the agenda calls for a brief presentation of the report by eva lichtenberger, on behalf of the committee on transport and tourism, on the green paper on the future of ten-t policy (2008/2218 (ini)) (a6-0224/2009).
member of the commission. − mr president, since the trans-european transport network policy was established 15 years ago, it has contributed significantly to the functioning of the internal market and to economic, social and territorial cohesion. it now needs to be adjusted to new challenges. the green paper on the ten-t policy review addresses these challenges and proposes measures to tackle them at both the network planning and the project implementation stages. the commission appreciates very much that the european parliament is following this revision process from the outset, as reflected in this resolution. this underlines the determination of both institutions to develop a future-oriented ten-t policy. there is a high degree of conformity between our proposals and the objectives and calls set out in ms lichtenberger’s report as adopted by the committee on transport: that is, a more integrated and coherent network approach is necessary, in which intermodal connections such as rail connections to ports and airports and intermodal terminals, the link between long-distance and urban transport systems as well as interoperability must be strengthened so as to improve the basis for efficient, safe and high-quality services for passengers and for freight transport. the commission also shares the view set out in the report that – in particular in the freight sector – it is vital to facilitate co-modal chains in which waterborne and rail transport play an important role and intelligent transport systems help to optimise infrastructure use. in the draft report, the transport committee has chosen option three, a dual layer consisting of a core and a comprehensive network. by supporting this option, parliament confirms the need to combine traditional transport infrastructure policy with an appropriate consideration of new conditions and circumstances; the need for more flexibility and responsiveness to changing situations and more openness for the identification and support of infrastructure measures resulting for transport service requirements; and the economic and environmental challenge to promote a coordinated improvement of transport corridors through a series of small infrastructures and its projects. we note that, after the vote on the draft report by the transport committee, an alternative resolution has been proposed which supports option two, a single-layer network with priority projects or a priority network only, and therefore without a comprehensive network. this is, as we see it, in contradiction with some other points of the draft resolution. i would also like to recall on this occasion the advantages and disadvantages of the comprehensive network. while being too large to allow for clear priority-setting and the focus of community instruments to stimulate its implementation, it contributes to ensuring the ten-t access function and to facilitating cohesion. it has also proved to be vital as a reference framework for various transport policy actions and legislation: in particular, interoperability in the railway sector and road safety. elimination of the comprehensive network would therefore have some perverse effects. on the network implementation side, we fully agree with the view set out in the report that member states have a crucial role in deciding, planning and financing transport infrastructure. sufficient financial resources are needed under the ten-t budget and coordination of territorial development objectives and ten-t policy need to be enforced, whereas public/private partnerships have to be further promoted. the commission also underlines that ten-t investment is key to sustainable economic development and thus is an essential way of helping to overcome the current crisis. to conclude, we are very grateful for the motion for a resolution on the future of the trans-european transport networks policy. we would like to thank the transport committee for its constructive debate on it, and in particular ms lichtenberger for her comprehensive work. it will constitute a valuable contribution to the next steps of the process in the debates with the other institutions.
the point is closed. the vote will take place on wednesday 22 april 2009. the commission shall be assisted by the committee of the regions.

the agenda calls for the joint debate on:- the report by jean-paul gauzès, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on credit rating agencies (com ((2008) 0704 - c6-0397/2008 - 2008/0217 ((cod)) (a6-0191/2009),- the report by renate weber, on behalf of the committee on legal affairs, on the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council amending directives 77/91/eec, 78/855/eec and 82/891/eec and council directive 2005/56/ec as regards reporting and documentation obligations in the event of mergers or divisions (com ((05762008) - c6-0330/2008 - 2008/0182 ((cod)) (a6-0247/2009), and the report by peter skinner, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council amending directive 2007/138/ec on direct business reinsurance and access to financial services (com (a03-0231/2008) and amended by the committee on economic and monetary affairs) (com (2006-0146-0131 (a04)).
the rapporteur. - madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the report on rating agencies which i have been asked to draw up has been a particularly interesting one to draw up, and i am particularly pleased that we have been able to reach agreement with the council and the commission so that this report has a chance of being adopted at first reading. the analysis of the various causes of the financial crisis has shown that there is a need and an urgency to regulate credit rating agencies. the commission's proposal for a regulation has been examined very carefully by parliament to ensure that european regulation is both exemplary, effective and pragmatic. the recent conclusions of the g20 have further strengthened this determination. the compromise reached by the commission, the eu presidency and parliament is in line with the guidelines sought by parliament on the essential points of this regulation: the scope of application, the rating of third countries and the prevention of conflicts of interest. but i am particularly pleased that this text has laid the foundations for european supervision in the spirit of the de larosière report. parliament has insisted that the cesr should be the single entry point for the registration of agencies. we knew that in the present state of the law it was not possible to do much more, but we have thus laid the foundations for this european supervision in the future. in the coming months, the commission will propose a legislative initiative to implement the guidelines of the de larosière report, in order to create an effective and coordinated european supervision. pending the commission's legislative initiative, regulation will be carried out temporarily, under the coordination of cesr, by a college composed of representatives of the competent authorities of the member states, with the legal force of decisions being ensured by the competent authority of the place where the agency has its seat. i would like to say today how much parliament appreciated the very constructive and cooperative attitude of the czech presidency in the second phase of the negotiations. we have therefore been able, through a clever work of thought, to develop a number of rules which should make it possible to ensure this necessary transparency and to remedy the difficulties and dysfunctions which have resulted from the lack of regulation of the rating agencies. this is therefore a very satisfactory result, and that is why a comprehensive amendment will be tabled in parliament tomorrow, incorporating the text agreed by the commission, parliament and the czech presidency, i.e. the member states. i believe that in this way the european parliament, the commission and the presidency will have shown that, in the face of a crisis of unprecedented proportions, the european institutions have been very responsive. i hope that in the same spirit the other provisions of this financial package, and in particular the recast of the directive on the capital adequacy of banks, also known as basel ii, can be adopted. at a time when europeans are questioning the effectiveness of europe, it seems to me essential that we can prove that europe is there in the face of the crisis.
for the greens/efa group madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would first like to say that i fully agree with mr mitchell's statement. we're not in the timing, we're not in the rhythm. i would point out to him, however, that the same mistake should not be made with regard to the french president as the french sometimes make with regard to mr gordon brown. it is not talk about action that guarantees the effectiveness of action. on the crisis itself, it is clear that for us, the crisis is not the starting point of finance. it's rooted in social and environmental issues. but it combines with the financial cycle, which is that when things are going well, we take risks, and when things are not going well, we think that maybe we should regulate a little. we're in that phase where we have to regulate, and we have to regulate hard. we need to regulate at the level of the single market, which means that we need much more centralised regulation at the european level. that's what guides us in our voting choices. we are in full agreement with the gauzès report and the progress it has made, and we have been calling for more centralised regulation and supervision at european level for years, and the first step taken with the cesr seems to us to be quite right. but despite mr skinner's efforts - and here we agree exactly with mr mitchell's criticism - we regret that the governments have not understood. we do not agree with the compromise which is being proposed and which rejects the system of group supervision. i think that such a method will lead to new disasters. so we will vote against the skinner report, not against mr skinner's work itself, but against the compromise imposed by governments.
madam president, the reports by mr gauzès on credit rating agencies, by mrs weber on reporting obligations in respect of mergers and acquisitions, and by mr skinner on the pursuit of insurance or reinsurance activities contain useful provisions, but they cannot be described as measures to combat the financial crisis. the crisis we are experiencing is obviously of a completely different scale and cannot be solved simply by these technical and ad hoc measures. what is needed to solve the terrible crisis we are experiencing? first of all, we must break with the dogmas on which you have operated up to now, that is to say, the dogmas which believe in the beneficence of the international division of labour, the free movement of people, goods and capital. the free movement of goods, which has put european workers in competition with workers in countries which, like communist china, are the paradise of the most cynical capitalism, where workers have no right to strike, no trade union freedoms, no adequate pensions, no social protection, and have absolutely ridiculous wage levels. but it's not the only state in this situation. the free movement of people, which has led us, which has led you, to accept and still advocate, as the only alternative for future generations, a policy of mass immigration, the disastrous results of which are now clearly visible. and finally, the free movement of capital, which was the trigger for the crisis, since it allowed the crisis in the mortgage market and the acquisition of individual property in the united states of america - which was a purely circumstantial crisis, which should have remained confined to the american market - to contaminate virtually all our economies and ruin our savers, our employees, our entrepreneurs. so we must free small and mediumsized enterprises from the shackles of taxation and bureaucracy; simple rules are needed to ensure that monetary values actually correspond to the real industrial or service heritage; we must have an investment policy, but a profitable investment policy. these are some of the essential measures which we would like to see taken by the governments of the member states as part of those national policies which have proved their superiority in terms of responsiveness.
madam president, on solvency ii, this is a reform that was initiated long before the crisis and that the crisis has brought to light. as legislators we hesitated: should we have concluded this agreement at first reading? finally, the negotiators' determination has led to a compromise which i believe has at least two merits: first, to force the insurance sector to better assess its risks, which until now has been the subject of relatively old mechanisms and probably not adapted to what has become the reality of the insurance sector, and secondly to emphasize the need for supervisory mechanisms to adapt to what has become the insurance companies, both in their multitude of products and offers to the consumer, but also in their transnational presence. as legislators we have been keen to take account of the reality of this market, that is to say a market where, for example, in some countries there are life insurance schemes which represent a significant part of this sector and where, in the light of the crisis, we had to take account of what procyclicality means when it applies to the insurance sector. we also had to ensure that the adoption of this legislation did not upset the architecture of the insurance market and, in particular, allowed the structures of mutual societies to find their place within this legislation. but of course this is only a first step, and i would like to mention six points on which we must start work immediately tomorrow. the first is, of course, to take account of the conclusions of the jacques de larosière report and the need to ensure that there is equality and harmonious conditions between the various colleges of supervisors and, to this end, to strengthen the european authority responsible for the supervision of insurance companies. secondly, as many colleagues have said, we must set up this so-called support group, and on this point i do not share alain lipietz's opinion. of course, we would have preferred to have had the support of the group, but how can we fail to understand that in countries where 80 or 100% of the insurance sector is in the hands of foreign companies, without a clear legal basis, it is now difficult to accept this mechanism? we must make progress on this. the third step for tomorrow is to harmonize what we do here with what is happening with the pension funds. how can we imagine that insurance requires improved solvency, and not ask the question for pension funds? this is an absolutely major challenge. the fourth area of work for tomorrow is the installation, the creation, the establishment of a deposit guarantee mechanism, such as we have today in the banking sector, and which is still lacking in the insurance sector. fifthly, the marketing of insurance products and ensuring that the way in which insurance intermediaries offer products to insured persons takes account of their interests and protection needs. finally, the transposition into this sector of what we are going to put in place for the banking sector, namely the retention mechanisms for securitisation. on this basis, i hope that tomorrow we will be able to take account of the lessons of this crisis and ensure that the european citizens have an insurance sector which is a real guarantee for them to... the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner tajani, ladies and gentlemen, the two principles which have guided my approach since the beginning of the process have been the equalization of passenger rights in all modes of transport, which is an objective which the commission and the european parliament have set themselves, and the fact of ensuring that these rights, with special attention to persons with reduced mobility - because indeed there was a certain lag in the world of maritime transport towards these people - are strongly inscribed in this text. the general spirit of the text is that we can travel in europe without being subject to the good will of the airlines, that we can demand a minimum of services, a minimum of information and, finally, that disabled passengers, the pmr, can enjoy the same quality of rights as other european citizens and that they are not penalized twice. the text adopted by the commission on 31 march seems to be consistent with the overall approach. firstly, because we are increasing the rights of people with reduced mobility. if this text is adopted, no one will be refused entry on the grounds of disability, with the exception of, of course, the conditions of boarding, respect for the dignity of the person and the technical features of the ship. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. today, thanks to the network and the internet, we need and it is necessary to have round trips and information that is formalized. so this has been dealt with in the text. finally, information on passenger rights, as it exists today in railways and in air transport, must be standardised in accessible formats. as far as the rights of all passengers are concerned, we thought it important that compensation in the event of problems should also be harmonised upwards, taking as a basis what is done in the air. and, for that, delays, cancellations will allow refunds up to 100% with a grid based on problems. information should be clear and available, which is often a problem in transport. we see it regularly, people lack information, they do not know why the boat, in this case - the committee on budgets - mr president, yes, i am replacing mrs sartori, who is indeed detained in italy, and it is true that i am very sorry to have to say this to you because she would have particularly liked to be here today. medical procedures are the subject of our discussion, especially because they can sometimes have harmful consequences for the health of patients, either because of adverse effects of medication, medical errors, or infections contracted in medical facilities. these risks include, in particular, hospital-acquired infections, which affect one in 20 patients admitted to hospital, or 4 100 000 per year. the figures from the european commission on this subject are very worrying. adverse events occur in 8% to 12% of patients hospitalized in the member states of the european union. this translates into an annual number of between 7 million and 15 million patients in hospital, plus some 37 million patients in primary health care. infections in hospitals alone affect on average one in 20 patients admitted to hospital, for a total of over 4 million patients per year. in total, hospital-acquired infections cause the death of around 37 000 people in europe each year. to achieve the objective of reducing these infections by 900 000 cases per year by 2015, i.e. a reduction of 20%, the member states and the european institutions are called upon to put in place the necessary instruments. the report recommends: to promote the education and training of health and paramedical personnel, with particular attention to hospital-acquired infections and the antiviral resistance of the viruses that cause them; to improve patient awareness of this problem by asking the commission to develop a document for patients based on a practical guide for the prevention of hospital-acquired infections that was developed by the world health organisation who in 2003; support research in this field with particular attention to new technologies, nanotechnologies and nanomaterials; increase the presence of nurses specialised in infection control. finally, as the text emphasizes, and as mrs sartori has stressed, it is important to improve patient education on this subject. it is imperative to invite the commission to draw up a document for the prevention of these hospital-acquired infections for use by patients and to submit it to parliament and the council. the commission will also have to monitor progress made by the member states and the european union in this area every three years. a survey carried out in france, for example, shows that 83% of the respondents have heard of hospital-acquired infections, and that these risks are the main source of concern for french people in the context of hospitalization. in contrast, the general public does not feel adequately informed about the causes and consequences of hospital-acquired infections. the effort to control hospital-acquired infections will have to be more focused in the coming years on informing health professionals and the general public.

in writing. bus and coach passengers should enjoy the same rights as air and rail passengers. that is the philosophy behind this report. in principle, all passengers must be equal before the law. however, there are many reservations. they are linked to the very nature of this sector, which is dominated by micro-enterprises and smes. we cannot be satisfied with measures such as those proposed in plenary which, under the pretext of greater protection of passenger rights, merely introduce unmanageable constraints on bus and coach drivers and unavoidable price increases for passengers themselves. why should a driver whose job is to drive safely be required to undergo special training to provide assistance to people with reduced mobility or disabilities? why not clearly exempt from the scope of this new european regulation scheduled urban, suburban and regional transport services, which are themselves covered by public service contracts? why should we want to introduce compensation rights of up to 200% of the ticket price in the event of denied boarding due to overbooking? in france, the national federation of passenger transport offered pragmatic solutions to all these problems. some of them were heard. not all of them. that's too bad.
in writing. i voted against the report on crossborder health services because it does not meet the eu's objective of a high level of health, as set out in article 152 of the treaty, and the demand of european citizens to be able to benefit from quality and safe healthcare close to home. the report does not make prior authorisation the rule for being able to receive treatment in another eu member state. prior authorisation allows the financial balance of social systems to be checked and the patient to be guaranteed reimbursement conditions and the necessary information before a hospital intervention abroad. it is also unacceptable that the quality of health care should be improved by competing with other providers of care or by taking as a principle the free movement of patients, which depends primarily on their state of health. the amendments voted on are too vague, paving the way for the court of justice of the eu to resolve the problems. this directive only increases health inequalities among european citizens, because only those who can afford health care will be able to choose quality services.
the president-in-office of the council. − mr president, madam member, ladies and gentlemen, on 2 april 2009, the g20 heads of state and government met in london to discuss the next steps towards the recovery of the world economy and the prevention of future crises of the present scale. at their meeting, the heads of state and government committed themselves to doing all that is necessary to restore confidence, economic growth and employment, to repair the financial system so that credit flows are restored, to strengthen financial regulation and restore market confidence, and to finance and reform our international financial institutions so that they can effectively help to overcome this crisis and prevent future crises. at the same time, heads of state and government committed to promote global trade and investment, reject protectionism and prepare the economy for inclusive, environmentally friendly and sustainable recovery and growth, in order to enhance prosperity. the eu and its proposals and positions have played a very important role. in many, if not most, areas, the eu and the european members of the g20 were the driving force or one of the driving forces behind the work of the preparatory groups and significantly influenced both the breadth of consensus reached and the final shape of the agreed proposals. this included financial market regulation, supervision and transparency of the financial system, rejection of protectionism, pushing for the completion of the doha development agenda, an approach to economic recovery including emphasis on the need to transition the financial sector by cleaning up depreciating assets and laying the foundations for a future sustainable global economy. last but not least, it was the commitment of the eu countries to provide a financial injection to the international monetary fund that not only influenced the willingness of other countries to make similar commitments, but above all played an important, if not a key role, in deciding that the stabilisation of economies that cannot help themselves will not be guided by ad hoc solutions and bilateral aid, but that we will systematically use the multilateral institutions that we have for this purpose, and that in this regard we will also restore respect and authority to them alongside financial strengthening. so let me take a step back and look at what the g20 london summit could mean for the world economy and specifically for the european union. i'll start with a memory of 1933. in june 1933, representatives of 66 countries met in london to try to devise a common plan to restore the world economy in the midst of the great depression. the london monetary and economic conference, which set out to revive global trade, stabilize prices, and restore the gold standard as the basis of the monetary system, was organized by the league of nations and met in a similar global economic situation to the one we are experiencing today. within a month, however, the conference ended in failure and a subsequent loss of confidence, further economic collapse and a chain of devaluations of currencies to strengthen their own economy at the expense of others. european countries turned inward, the american economy became isolated, and that lasted for many years. as the recession turned into a deep depression, unemployment grew and social tensions and the political fallout of tensions led to world war ii. in the weeks leading up to the london summit in 2009, it was difficult not to recall the analogy with the london summit in 1933. fortunately, the world seems to have learned from the experience, at least for now. after many months of disappointed expectations and hopes, low market confidence and a deepening recession, it was almost a political imperative that the g20 summit end on a high note. it was a nightmare task, given how widely different the expectations of different groups and different countries were, and given that some of these expectations were not entirely realistic. it is too early, ladies and gentlemen, to judge whether the g20 heads of state and government meeting has been a success. however, the weeks that have passed since the summit have given us cause for cautious optimism that the summit has indeed been a turning point in this global recession and that it may also become a key historical event in global economic cooperation. it also has a chance to stand the test of time and make history in a way that is as significant as the 1944 bretton woods conference, some of whose outcomes determined the shape of global economic cooperation for a quarter of a century and others that continue to shape it for 60 years. the historic importance of the groundwork laid at the london g20 summit will only be seen when all the commitments made at that summit have been fulfilled, if at all. despite this necessary reservation, there are four reasons why the g20 london meeting can be seen as a successful start to economic recovery and to a new, more sustainable form of global economy and global economic decision-making. first, the g20 summit has indeed boosted confidence in the economy and in the markets. so far, this confidence-building has not been dizzying, and it is natural that it will take time for confidence to be fully restored. the most significant aspect of confidence-building was the way in which the g20 summit participants acted. in the face of deep global decline, they have remained united and reached a broad consensus. key to confidence in the current period of uncertainty was also that the summit participants reaffirmed some fundamental economic paradigms: at the core, at the heart of our global recovery plan, must be jobs, the needs and interests of people who are not afraid of work, all over the world, not only in rich countries but also in poor countries. at the heart of our plan for global recovery must be the needs and interests of not only people active today, but also future generations. recovery cannot be at the expense of the interests of our children and grandchildren. the only reliable basis for sustainable globalisation and growing prosperity is an open world economy based on market principles, effective regulation and strong global institutions. second, the g20 summit sent a very strong signal, perhaps the strongest in 60 years, that the world is returning to multilateralism in economic decision-making on matters of global reach. at the end of the summit, the heads of state or government declared their conviction that prosperity is indivisible and that for economic growth to be sustainable, it must be shared by states. if there is one lesson we can take from the current global crisis, it is that in our economic destiny, we are all connected. we're in the same boat, small and big countries, open or isolated. the interconnectedness of our economies, especially over the last 10 to 15 years, has brought us tremendous benefits in the form of long periods of no major conflict, in the form of unprecedented economic prosperity, the fastest global economic growth in human history, in the form of hundreds of millions of people getting a chance to get out of extreme poverty. it has brought expanded markets for our manufacturers, low inflation and low unemployment. we should not give up these advantages at any cost. this inevitably requires coordination of our policies, in good times and in bad, and the g20 summit confirmed this recognition. thirdly, heads of state and government have reached consensus on issues where a year ago, or nine months ago, consensus would have been almost unthinkable. the london commitments have concluded three months of intensive discussions at the working level and are truly groundbreaking. if they are fulfilled and put into practice, they will certainly provide a good basis for prevention so that we can avoid similarly devastating crises in the coming decades. fourth, the summit has reshaped the space for global economic cooperation, leading to a new balance of power. the largest emerging economies have been given full recognition for their role in the global economy. developed countries and emerging economies have also come together to recognize that the stability and prosperity of poor countries and the most vulnerable social groups everywhere in the world is in the best interest of all of us. this is a strategically significant change. for europe, this means that it will have to fight with a new vision and a well-thought-out policy to maintain its position in global economic decision-making. the size of the eu economy and the legacy of the past alone will not be enough to maintain its important strategic role in the global economic decision-making system in the future. however, from the eu's point of view, the outcome of the london summit was an undeniable success. the summit agreed on all the priorities agreed by the eu heads of state or government in the european council conclusions of 19 and 20 march 2009. the london g20 summit rejected protectionism, committed to responsible and sustainable economic policies, supported multilateralism and agreed to all priorities for financial sector regulation that eu member states collectively considered essential. as mentioned above, in a number of areas, eu members have been the key drags of the g20 negotiations, or one of the drags. however, a number of issues remain open following the london g20 summit. first, despite the enormous progress made in financial regulation and supervision in recent months, a number of issues are still at an incomplete stage and work is continuing. at eu level, however, there is a clear roadmap and timetable for the next two months and a division of roles between the european commission, the european central bank, the european financial commission, ecofin and the june european council. this programme includes, inter alia, the immediate task of taking decisive steps in the area of accounting standards that will enable european banks to operate on a level playing field with american banks. second, on global trade, the g20 leaders in london reaffirmed their previous commitment from washington not to create new barriers to trade. the g20 also reaffirmed its commitment to complete the doha development agenda with an ambitious and balanced outcome. but this commitment was also made at the g20 summit last november, where heads of state and government even committed to reaching the doha development agenda by the end of 2008. the question therefore remains how serious this commitment is this time. however, the g20 leaders in london have now declared that they will give the doha development agenda their personal attention from now on and that they will ensure that it also receives political attention at all forthcoming international meetings that are relevant in this regard. for the eu, pushing for these agreements must be a key priority. third, the g20 committed to provide $1.1 trillion through the international monetary fund and multilateral development banks to support the restoration of credit flows, economic growth and jobs in the global economy. the details of this commitment are yet to be agreed and clarified. the commitment has a short, medium and long-term phase, and the short-term phase also includes the eur 75 billion pledged by the eu countries to the international monetary fund to restore balance of payments stability in the event of an acute need. the details of this commitment are not yet worked out, and the finance ministers of our countries must work out the form and mechanism of this commitment. as for the medium and long-term commitments to strengthen multilateral institutions, this includes a commitment to provide the international monetary fund with an unprecedented $500 billion multilateral loan. in addition, the london summit led to a commitment by g20 countries to support the new issue of sdrs (special drawing rights), the imf's own currency, which imf member countries can use to make payments to each other. the commitment is for 250 billion sdrs. both multilateral credit and sdr issuance will require both rather complicated technical designs and the approval of the imf's authorised bodies, negotiations with the participating countries and ratification of agreements by the national parliaments of the member countries. all of this may take several years, so we need to be firm but realistic in our expectations. the above commitments were also linked to an agreement that the g20 countries would do their utmost to swiftly implement the april 2008 reform of the decision-making structure of the international monetary fund, which has so far been held back by slow ratification by national parliaments. the g20 also asked the international monetary fund to accelerate the next round of membership share and voting rights reforms to be ready by january 2011. this forthcoming reform needs to be given due attention by eu countries, as it could result in many, perhaps most, eu countries losing the direct and indirect participation of their national envoys in the imf's decision-making process and direct access to information. moreover, the reform will take place in the context of the imf's increasing role in global economic decision-making. until now, this issue has been on the fringe of attention in many eu member states, but it should not escape their scrutiny and attention in the coming months. fourthly, there remains one area which will need to be seriously and thoroughly discussed and addressed. that's the global imbalance and the question of the entire global monetary system of the future. these issues were not on the agenda of the london summit consciously and deliberately and so they remain on the list of areas where work is still ahead of us. in this context, it is worth recalling that it was the failure to reach agreement on a global monetary order that brought down the london summit of 1933. today, the question is no simpler than it was then. the eu must give this issue due attention, as addressing it remains one of the important ingredients of sustainable economic recovery and prevention of devastating global crises. in conclusion, ladies and gentlemen, let me thank the united kingdom, the g20 presidency, for organising the summit and, in particular, for organising the whole process of discussions and negotiations at working level in the weeks and months leading up to the summit. the organisers have done a great job and deserve our high praise for their considerable contribution to the progress made and the extent of the consensus reached. it is hoped that the g20 summit in london will usher in a new and successful era of global economic cooperation. we believe he has a very good chance. the conclusions of the g20 summit in london are a very good starting point for ending the global economic crisis as soon as possible. it has also opened up the possibility of reshaping the future global connected economy to better prepare it for the long-term sustainable production of economic decision-making coordination. there remains a vast unfinished agenda and commitments that will have to be fulfilled. the coming months and years will tell how much of the london summit will go down in history. in any case, the g20 summit has been dedicated to changing strategic positions in the global economy. it is important for the eu to enter this period with a clear and realistic vision and with policies that will ensure that the european economy continues to play the strategic role it has enjoyed so far and that the 500 million eu citizens deserve.

the commission has already submitted a proposal for a directive on the marketing of construction products. i would like to thank the commission for its technical support and all the fictitious rapporteurs for their willingness and their spirit of dialogue, which has gradually brought us closer together on important points and positions on this dossier. while we fully support the objectives of the reform, which are better functioning of the market, more credibility for the ce marking, simplification of the system, and we share the undoubted interest in having a common technical language, a large majority of our members in the imco committee were keen to express their doubts. these doubts are primarily due to our unanimous desire to avoid simplifying and relaxing procedures which would lead to a change in the control and declaration of products. they also concern the position of the commission, which in our view tends to be satisfied with a situation where the choice of the criteria for evaluating products is partly left to the member states, which varies the actual meaning of the ce marking according to the country where the products are placed on the market, with problematic consequences in terms of credibility. finally, our reservations are based on the fact that, at a time when we want to put europe on the path to a green economy, the text proposed to us does not deal with the energy performance of products or even their partial danger to users. to address these concerns, the imco committee has introduced a series of amendments. i'll take five of them myself. firstly, we propose to maintain the requirement that all construction products placed on the market bear the ce marking in order to ensure that everything sold in europe has undergone the appropriate control procedures. this choice must not contribute to increasing the burden on the most fragile firms and thereby hampering their activity. that is why we have advocated the maintenance of simplified procedures for micro-enterprises and introduced a measure to exclude small craftsmen from the compulsory ce marking. the second point concerns the simplified procedures for easier access to the ce marking. however, we have chosen to restrict access to manufacturers of construction products, not to importers. this approach, which aims to improve market surveillance, will help to avoid the import of lower quality products via dubious importing companies. third major change, the introduction of a minimum level of harmonisation in the evaluation criteria for construction products in europe, so that the ce marking can have the same meaning regardless of the country where the product is marketed. we want the requirements for evaluating a product in europe to be common to all member states wherever possible. in this context, we have also introduced the possibility of creating new evaluation criteria which are not merely technical but which allow for the measurement of performance in relation to issues of general interest, such as the environment, safety or health risk. in the same spirit - and this will be my fourth point - we have contributed to a high-level reinforcement of the information transmitted to the user by the manufacturer through the declaration of performance. in particular, the manufacturer will be required to declare any dangerous substance now listed in an annex which also includes the elements mentioned in the reach directive. finally, and this is my final point, the members of the imco committee have sought to introduce a higher level of transparency as regards the conditions for the certification of construction products, more transparency as regards the place of undertakings in the certification process, and more transparency also as regards the clarification of the conditions for access to the ce marking, clearly distinguishing the access routes for products covered by a harmonised standard from the road routes for products which are not covered by a harmonised standard and which have often been described as innovative products. this work is indeed coming to a close, but it has not yet reached the point where we wanted to be. the difficulties encountered in the council with regard to the elaboration of a position did not allow it to be carried out, despite good cooperation by the french and czech presidencies. i regret that today, knowing that the time we have now thanks to the additional time may allow us, at second reading, to reach a much wider consensus, but above all, of course, to deepen our exchanges, which will make these positions for this sector more effective.

the rapporteur. - mr president, i would first like to thank the fictitious rapporteurs who contributed to the adoption of this report in the committee on economic and monetary affairs, mrs pietikäinen and mrs raeva in particular, and to congratulate the coordinators of the epp and liberal groups, mr gauzès and mr klinz, who played an important role in the adoption of this report in the committee on economic and monetary affairs, which will be put to the vote in our plenary tomorrow. you know that at the end of the g20, a number of heads of state, not least in the european union, shouted victory, announcing, with much communication, that the era of banking secrecy was over. beyond these loud declarations, the european parliament, and i am glad of it, has moved on to practical work and has focused, rather than on communication, on how it could try to combat effectively tax evasion, which is estimated to amount to 200 billion euros each year, 200 billion euros which must be brought closer to what the european countries' recovery plans were in the face of the crisis, 200 billion euros which must be brought closer to the european union's budget, 200 billion euros which must also be brought closer to the level of the european countries' deficits. the european taxpayers are now perfectly justified in calling on the european banking sector, and therefore on european banks, to make efforts to enable the tax administrations of the member states to recover part of the tax revenues that have been stolen from them by evasion or fraud. we had a job that was constructive work and i think it avoided sinking into the ukase or the denunciation of each other. we have made progress in three directions, and i want to welcome the text proposed by the european commission and the work done by commissioner kovács, which was undoubtedly in the right direction. we have tried, to the best of our ability, in line with what the european taxpayers tell us, to improve the commission's text in three ways. we felt that, within the scope of the directive, the text was a little too timid, both in terms of the legal structures involved and in the definition of savings products. we know that financial engineering has a considerable imagination when it comes to inventing new financial products to enable certain individuals to escape taxation, hence the proposal by parliament and the commission to set up a comitology procedure which adapts the definition of savings products to what is now the reality of financial engineering. but in this respect many products are currently excluded from the scope and, in our view, should be integrated as soon as possible; this is particularly the case for certain forms of retirement savings which operate by capitalisation, and more generally we believe that the proposal to include products which guarantee 95% of the investment do not offer sufficient guarantees. that is why the 90% threshold seems more reasonable to us. amendments to this effect will be tabled in plenary tomorrow. we'll see if they're adopted. i regret that we have not found a compromise on this point in committee, and i hope that the plenary will send a strong signal by defining savings products as products which guarantee 90% of the capital and not just 95%, as the commission proposes. one point, however, has led to a broad consensus on how to extend the scope of the directive, particularly in the drafting of annexes i and iii. the report also considerably strengthens annex i, since we have drawn up a very broad list of tax havens which does not spare any jurisdiction, including delaware and nevada, unlike the g20 list. we are putting the burden of proof on these courts that legal constructions defined in a broader way than the commission either do not exist in their territory or are tax transparently transparent, and i believe that this inversion of the burden of proof is a more effective way of fighting tax evasion. the main weakness of this text, however - and i conclude here - concerns the transitional period granted to three member states: belgium, austria and luxembourg. even though belgium has announced that it will abandon the withholding tax, i want the automatic exchange of information to be generalized and, in order for it to be generalized, a deadline to be set for the end of the transition period, and that is why, even though we have adopted the principle of a study assessing the respective merits of the withholding tax and the exchange of information for 2011, at the time of the revision of the directive, we want a deadline to be set for 2014 to end this transition period. i mean we tried to work in a spirit of transparency and improved transparency at a time when european taxpayers are being called upon to contribute, in particular to the rescue of the european banking sector.

the rapporteur. - madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, tomorrow we shall be voting on the telecoms package, the final step in months of work and negotiations to reach this compromise, which was achieved after a great deal of struggle with the council in a context where the three institutions were taking divergent positions. i would like to begin by sincerely thanking my colleagues del castillo, harbour, pleguezuelos, the fictitious rapporteurs, the political groups, the committee chairmen and their secretariats, the council presidency and the european commission for their hard work over these long months, and i thank all the colleagues who have chosen to trust me and support me. the advances made possible by this package are many. they are about consumers, offering them better services at fairer prices. telecommunications are characterised by their impact on daily life and play an obvious social role as a vehicle for development and growth. the telecommunications sector alone provides more than 3.5 million jobs and represents an increasing share of the european economy, at nearly 3.5%. well-regulated competition allows a balance between old and new operators and ensures significant growth in the sector through legal certainty, which in turn encourages investment. that is why, throughout this round of negotiations, we have fought, with my fellow rapporteurs and our fictitious rapporteurs, to make this a regulatory framework that benefits everyone. the itre committee, in april, approved the penultimate stage of the legislative process, adopting the overall compromise on my report and that of pilar del castillo by a very large majority. we have laid the foundations for a solid compromise which i hope will receive your full support in the vote tomorrow, as will the reports by malcolm harbour and francisca pleguezuelos. i would also like to return to amendment no 138/46 and clarify the meaning and scope of the text on which parliament and the council agreed, the so-called 'last-chance compromise'. the council has consistently rejected this amendment from the moment it was voted at first reading, by removing it from its common position and refusing to mention it in the recitals or articles. the european parliament showed its support for this amendment by including in the compromise the key elements of amendment 46: defence of freedoms, right to a trial and recourse to a court - the expression most consistent with that of the judicial authority - and introduced two additional provisions for internet users: the affirmation of the indispensable nature of the internet for the exercise of fundamental rights and freedoms, specified with reference to the european convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. the spirit and the letter of amendment no 46 have thus been respected and extended to the benefit of users, and the rejection of this amendment by the member states on the grounds that the european parliament cannot impose on them a change in their internal legal system which would be necessary for the application of this amendment has been avoided. its place in article 1 concerning scope and objectives gives this proposal the meaning of a principle valid for all the directives of the package, in particular for access and services. the legal weakness created by the linking of amendment no 46 to article 8, which defines the tasks of the national regulators, is thus resolved. we are faced, ladies and gentlemen, with a choice: to support amendment no 46 as it stands, with the consequence of referring the whole telecom package to conciliation which will reopen the discussion on all the achievements of the negotiations and will lead to its withdrawal because of the massive opposition of the member states to this amendment, or to support the new wording of amendment no 46, which guarantees respect for fundamental freedoms, thus confirming what parliament adopted when voting on the lambrinidis report. i would add that the presence of article 1 (3a) and its recital will have to be taken into account in the transposition of the directive and will enable parliament to legislate subsequently. in view of this choice, i would ask you, ladies and gentlemen, to think about the future of our work in the next parliamentary term, which will concern, among other things, the universal service but also content and intellectual property, and i would therefore ask you to support the new proposal, in order to treat the rights of employees, artists and internet users on an equal footing.

the rapporteur. - madam president, thank you very much, commissioner, for your statement which sheds a very positive light on the debate which has just taken place, and i thank all the members who have spoken. i would like to say that our parliament, by voting this compromise on the telecom package, is clearly making a choice. it is a regulated market, not a market without rules. it also shows a strategy, a development strategy that is useful in a crisis context and that prepares european society for the digital age. this vote will also ensure a balance between the prerogative of the states and the powers of the commission, between old operators and new entrants, thanks to the clauses which defend non-discrimination, but it will also mark progress for the european parliament itself in the exercise of its power of codecision, in particular in the area of spectrum allocation policy, which is considered a public good, and in its support, once again, for broadcasters and services. many colleagues have spoken on the issue of the internet as a public space, which as such requires - and i agree with them - freedom and security, hence the link between its accessibility and the fundamental rights of citizens, for the first time in a directive, with the new version of amendment no 46. the expression 'measures taken' is, in a sense, the missing link between any measures taken concerning electronic communications networks, whether cutting off or filtering, and the fundamental rights of users. and as regards the doubts of my colleagues about the rapporteur's willingness to defend a judgment before any cuts, i would like to say that the phrase 'independent and impartial tribunal' is a phrase which guarantees internet users the right to such a judgment. indeed, to demonstrate that hadopi is an independent and impartial tribunal would be to impose on that high authority all the obligations which a judge must respect: right of defence, adversarial procedure, publicity. it is obvious that this would lead to the implosion of a system which, in the french law as it is being debated, is essentially based on the automation and massification of charges and penalties. i therefore ask the european commission to exercise its utmost vigilance in the future transposition of this telecom package. when a fundamental principle is enshrined in a community text which is the subject of a compromise between the council and the european parliament as co-legislators, it must be correctly transposed into national law. and i would like to conclude, ladies and gentlemen, by saying that i welcome the possibility of a broad public consultation in the manner of the multi-partnership method, which will allow us to work on the basis of our hard work, within the framework of a compromise which respects the right expressed in amendment no 46 and makes it applicable.

in writing. under the pretext of revising authorised oenological practices, the european commission is preparing to authorise the blending of white and red wines under the name 'rosé wine'. i dispute the possibility of calling a blend of different wines "rosé". it is not the colour of the wine alone that should make its name: it is the grape varieties, the terroirs and the know-how of the winemakers that make the wines, not the final colour of any liquid. to make a rosé by cutting, it would be necessary to start from a white wine, more than 95%, which would be stained with red wine. rosé wine is made by fermenting grapes or red musts. thus, by allowing the cutting of wines, the european commission would be allowing a genuine counterfeit of rosé wine: it would be organizing a deception of consumers. apart from the insult to wine growers who are committed to a quality policy, particularly in provence, it would be unacceptable to legitimise a by-product from the mixture of finished products and to allow the misleading reference to the colour of rosé. if there is no other solution, these drinks should at least be labelled according to their actual content: 'cut wine' or 'mixed wine'.

the rapporteur. - mr president, after the big cake in the corbett report, i do not know if it is the cherry; it would be the little cake that you are given with the coffee, just to pass the addition. so i'm going to talk to you about petitions. we have noted in the past that the regulation as it was drafted presented us with some problems, because sometimes certain articles gave rise to difficult interpretations and even political blockages as to the admissibility of certain texts. we have therefore tried to do some cleaning up, clarifying, consolidating, but that does not constitute a revolution. we want to identify the petitioner better first, because at the moment, when we receive half a ton of petitions, we don't really know who the person to address is. we therefore ask petitioners to indicate who is their leader, so to speak, or else we shall decide to use the first name on the front page. we are instituting a right of withdrawal. we say to the citizens: "you can petition, but you can also waive this right and ask that your name be removed from the list of signatories". you know that our parliament can receive correspondence in minority languages when they are recognised by the states, such as galician, basque, catalan, etc. we have decided to extend this right to petitions as well. if you write to us in certain languages which the bureau has recognised as languages of written communication with the citizens, we will also reply in those languages. but the real reform is acceptability. until now, the members of the committee on petitions have sometimes been in a rather bitter fight over whether a text really concerns european law or not. finally, europe was everywhere, and by the roads, it was always possible to get there. so we tried to simplify things by giving a sort of eligibility bonus. if a quarter of the members of the committee on petitions think that a text is acceptable, it will be considered, because we are not talking about restricting an essential right, a right which is nevertheless based on primary law. in the event of a declaration of inadmissibility, we will even try to recommend some possible remedies. transparency is always at stake, as the name of the petitioner and the content of the petition will always be published in our records, but if, for reasons of privacy protection, the petitioner requests incognito, we can give him the right. the same applies if confidentiality is required for the proceedings. the right to speak is still maintained, of course, for the petitioners, at the discretion of the committee chairman. as for the right of follow-up, we have widened it a little - or rather clarified it - since before, the committee on petitions could rely on almost anything and everything for the preparation of an own-initiative report. we do not see why this committee should have more rights than the other committees. it obviously retains this right, provided that the conference of presidents of the political groups does not object. the electronic register is maintained. information missions go to the site, if necessary, to verify the facts or even to look for a possible solution. this is a somewhat new role of mediator which we have decided to introduce, and this can be a great credit to our parliament. we are asking the commission, represented at the highest level tonight, to help us, if necessary, to clarify the application of community law and, if necessary, to provide us with information. the information gathered is of course given to the commission, the council and the petitioner. but what if the lisbon treaty were to be ratified? you know that a new type of petition is provided for in this treaty - alongside the petition to the european parliament, which has now been in existence for a very long time - which is the petition to the european commission, with at least one million signatures. we simply decided that if a related issue were raised - in the event that the treaty of lisbon was ratified - by a petition submitted by a million citizens to the commission, we in parliament would check whether we were dealing with an identical subject and whether or not the petition addressed to the commission was likely to influence our own work, in which case we would simply inform the petitioners. i think that, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have pretty much summed up the situation. so there is no revolution, but clarification and the removal of any possible blockage.
the rapporteur. - mr president, i will try to answer my colleagues. jo, you're absolutely right, my tongue is out of joint. the procedures are quite different for referring the commission to the future provisions of the possible future treaty and for referring parliament to the petition procedure. but in the hypothetical case where these two types of interpellation, very different in terms of location and format, converged on the same subject, we decided that it was appropriate to alert the petitioners to establish whether or not there was a need to continue our investigations. in this case, we simply decided to develop coordination. i'm a good clarifier, but you were right to ask me for clarification on the linguistic level. i'm continuing my explanations on linguistics, as requested by costas. of course, there is no question of completing this tower of babel which is already very complex - just look at the number of interpreters who are still here tonight. it is noted that the bureau of parliament may decide that petitions and correspondence with petitioners shall be written in other languages used in a state. so these languages must have a place in the state and the state must demand it. this is the case for four languages so far, no more. if tomorrow i want to write in volapuk, which is an imaginary language, it is clear that no state will recognize it, and neither parliament nor its bureau will respond in that language. it's all very specific. as regards the problems of conflict between committees to which richard has drawn our attention, i would point out that my report states, again in accordance with rule 46 and annex vi, that the committee on petitions can already seek the opinion of another committee 'which has special competence for the matter under consideration'. you're saying that in that case, there may still be a conflict. well, we have appointed an arbiter, because the committee on petitions cannot take its own initiative or go against an own-initiative report of a committee responsible, unless the conference of presidents allows it. we have a point of reference, the conference of presidents, which will decide whether the committee on petitions or the committee responsible should take action, in the event that the two committees are unable to reach an agreement. so we've made sure that there's a backup. i think we can conclude on that, mr president. i have waited almost 20 years for the right to speak for six minutes in plenary. but in front of such an audience, it was really a pleasure.
on behalf of the ind/dem group. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, it is a good intention to want a recovery plan. keynesian recovery is necessary to meet a cyclical constraint, but here the crisis is structural. the tool is therefore inadequate. re-injecting funds into an extraverted economy is throwing money out the window. indeed, to revive an economy without having re-established community preference at our borders is to try to keep warm a house whose windows would be condemned to remain open. the consequences will be the exhaustion of the boiler and the explosion of the energy bill. after that preliminary, i would make three remarks. firstly, an energy market is irrelevant. in this case, competition does not lower prices, since they are determined by the cost of the means of production. we therefore feel it is essential to invest in really efficient energy sources, not to be fooled by heavily subsidised energy sources such as wind turbines, and to give preference to solar and nuclear energy. secondly, there is no efficiency in a single electricity market. over a large area, the energy consumption lost is proportional to the distance travelled. the probability of failure and disruption increases with the geographical complexity of the network. the interconnection of the european electricity grid must therefore return to its original function, which is to serve as a means of mutual assistance at the frontiers and to ensure, merely in the margin, an exchange of electricity. these works must be our priorities. thirdly, with regard to the podimata dossier, which is linked to this dossier, we would suggest that we should not only take into account the energy consumption required to operate a product, but also consider the information on the to us. it brings significant improvements to the dublin system, in particular from the point of view of respect for the fundamental rights of applicants for international protection. these include, in particular, the strengthening of the principle of family unity, increased attention to minors and the best interests of the child, better information and redress for applicants for international protection, strict limitation of the use of detention, and the possibility to temporarily suspend transfers to member states with particular pressure on their reception capacities or failing to ensure some points in the report remain problematic, notably the question of the language in which the information must be transmitted to the applicant. we think it must be a language that the person understands and not a language that he is supposed to understand. in the case of a person in detention, this is what the european convention on human rights provides. we also want the application of commission's original text, but the epp, supported by the rapporteur, opposed this proposal. finally, since the dublin regulation is not intended to ensure a fair sharing of responsibility for examining applications for international protection, it seems to me essential that other instruments be developed to strengthen solidarity - and you, commissioner barrot, have mentioned this - with the member states at the union's external borders.

the rapporteur. - mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, it is a great pleasure for me to present this evening the report on the financial aspects of the lisbon treaty which has been being prepared for some time in the committee on budgets. this will be the last budget report of this parliament and my last parliamentary report. above all, i am very pleased that parliament has had the courage to present our reports in the lisbon package to honour the promise to the citizens to inform them of the consequences of this treaty. a better informed citizen is a citizen who votes with knowledge. to speak of the lisbon treaty in this house is not to deny democracy, quite the contrary. its implementation will have important consequences for the budgetary powers of the institutions and financial implications. the reform is indeed far-reaching for parliament. apart from the introduction of multiannual financial frameworks, it should be remembered that the budgetary procedure has remained virtually unchanged since 1975. it was therefore essential that the committee on budgets should analyse these amendments and verify the conditions under which our institution could maintain or even strengthen its role as budgetary authority. that is the whole point of this report: simplification, clarification of the treaty's budgetary issues. i have been particularly concerned to defend the prerogatives of the parliamentary institution. future members must not be deprived of their powers in the next budgetary procedures and the next negotiations on the multiannual financial framework. these substantial changes are of three types. first, amendments to the primary law. the new budgetary procedure involves real progress and new challenges for parliament, starting with the abolition of the distinction between compulsory and non-compulsory expenditure. then, the introduction of a single reading for the budgetary procedure with the establishment of a mechanism of appeal in the event of rejection of the common position by the council, the setting up of a conciliation committee in charge of drawing up the common position and a tight timetable around this conciliation committee. the new multiannual financial framework also contains amendments which strengthen the role of parliament. this framework is becoming binding. its adoption requires unanimity in the council and the agreement of the european parliament. i would add that it was adopted following a special procedure, which is entirely new. as regards the new financial perspective, we want it to be five years long, to match the mandates of parliament and the european commission. the commissioners will thus be more responsible for the budgetary choices they make. the co-decision procedure is extended to the adoption of the financial regulation and the detailed rules for its application. but unfortunately the decision on own resources is still up to the council. parliament is merely consulted, except on the detailed rules for its application. budgetary discipline is therefore partly the responsibility of parliament, which can reject the multiannual financial framework. that's a real step up. the question for the next parliament is what will be negotiated under the new financial regulation procedure, on which parliament is a co-decision-maker, and what will be the legislation of the new regulation of the interinstitutional agreement, which parliament can simply reject or accept. finally, the union's new responsibilities will generate new financing needs: first, the external relations package, including the creation of the european external action service and the high representative vice-president of the commission, and then the new policies: energy, space and tourism, research, civil protection, administrative cooperation, sport. as you will have understood, ladies and gentlemen, the changes brought about by the treaty of lisbon are important.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the construction of europe sometimes gives rise to moving symbols for the anonymous actors we are. the final vote in the legislature will therefore be on what was the last amendment proposed jointly by meps and national meps before the european convention: the creation of a right of citizens' initiative at union level. let us not underestimate its significance. the treaty of lisbon gives the citizens themselves, ordinary citizens, the same power of political initiative as our own parliament has within the european union. our own-initiative reports enable us to invite the commission to act, to propose a legal basis for us to launch a new policy or to adapt an existing policy. well, citizens will be able to do the same, provided they are in sufficient numbers and come from a significant number of member states. i congratulate sylvia-yvonne kaufmann on the way she has worked to reach a consensus, which was obviously necessary on such a subject. the precision it gives to the treaty and the procedural guarantees are reasonable. the fixing of the significant number at one quarter of the member states is consistent with the solution chosen for the governments themselves in the framework of the area of freedom, security and justice. this new right, which has been given to european citizens, does not exist in this form in any of our countries. the union will also make progress in direct democracy. in france itself, for example, we dare not go that far. we reformed our national constitution last year, but by limiting such a right to collective petition to the local level only. let us now hope that our political parties will be able to compete in imagination to make the best use of this new right, and above all, beyond the parties, let us hope that civil society will take up this right: trade unions, non-governmental organisations, students - especially erasmus students - frontier workers, all european citizens who live in a country other than their country of origin and who find that the laws we vote on here are, alas, not being applied properly on the ground. in this union where everyone is free to move, the only barriers that remain are those of our political debates. once again, unfortunately, we are not starting a european election campaign, but 27 national campaigns on a european pretext. the economic area exists, the single currency exists, the single european sky exists, but the single political area has yet to be created. this is the real issue in the lisbon treaty, and this provision is certainly one of the most helpful.

vice-president of the commission. − mr president, i wish to thank the honourable members for this interesting debate, which has been partly consensual on a number of issues, partly a repetition of well-known arguments for and against the treaty, and partly a very interesting debate about what constitutes democracy. this is the first time i have heard about totalitarian systems that allow referendum after referendum in a number of member states, and why some referenda results are forgotten or do not count – mainly those that have meant a ‘yes’. it has also been a discussion about legitimacy. i still find it strange – and i have said this before – that a parliament like this one should say that a decision by a national parliament is anti-democratic or does not count or is not legitimate. as for the commission, it has always held the opinion that whatever system one chooses – a vote by referendum or through a national parliamentary decision – it is democratically legitimate. i do not see that any other position would be possible. any european citizen listening to this debate would wish us to go back to these reports, which actually reflect some serious concerns about the way we take decisions, about the rule book, about how to strengthen the democratic functioning of this european union, and about how to use the budget in the right way in order to put resources to our political priorities. all these things are taken up by these important reports. this is also about how to take decisions in an effective and hopefully more rapid way. i found mr lundgren’s intervention absolutely flabbergasting. do we really think the whole idea is to make things slower, and to slow down decision-making when dealing with an economic crisis like the one we are seeing now? people expect us to take action to ensure jobs and growth, to deal with climate change and the energy crisis and to tackle the problems that come with immigration and security – all of those things. that is the basis, also, for these reports. that is why we are here and that is how we gain democratic legitimacy – if we show that we can act and that we can act swiftly. i do not think that any arrogant, snobbish intervention, giving us lessons about this or that, helps us either. it is really about tackling these problems, which today are not national. they are european and international, and we have to have a modern rule book. we have to have a more democratic union which allows citizens to take the initiative. we never hear anything about that from those that are against. we never hear them say anything about the democratic strength of what is in the lisbon treaty; that is clearly missing. these reports give us a good grounding and a good platform to reform the way we work. from the commission’s side, we are of course willing to follow up and to work on all the details to ensure that we can implement this swiftly. a last point on ireland, is that after this ‘yes’ in the czech senate, all eyes will of course be on ireland again, and on the possibility of ratification by the end of the year. the issue of the legal guarantees is of course essential here, and both content and timing is very important. we are confident from the commission side that the eu council will be able to settle this issue, and i know also that careful preparations are taking place at the moment and we will, if given the possibility, also contribute from the commission side. thank you very much and thank you also for this being partly a social event, where people are thanking each other for the good cooperation and wishing all those who are leaving good luck. i guess we will all meet in the election campaign in one way or the other.
