in writing. two weeks ago the european parliament adopted a report on the common immigration policy for europe, laying the foundations for a massive immigration already planned by the european commission. today it's the turn of the asylum seekers. the aim is to establish a 'europe of asylum'. the clearly stated objective is to ensure that asylum seekers are treated to a higher standard of care in their reception conditions. this means not only standardizing minimum reception standards across all countries but also encouraging their mass installation. to this end, the scope of application of this future directive will be extended to all persons entering the territory of the union, whether legally or not. the administrative restrictions on access to the labour market in the member states will have to be removed. social, medical, psychological, housing and legal assistance must be provided by the host state. refusal of these grants will be subject to checks and legal remedies...which is often not the case for the nationals themselves... by adopting this second phase of the 'asylum package', brussels is facilitating and encouraging global immigration to europe. we will always oppose this globalist vision which has as its sole purpose the outright destruction of the peoples of europe and of the european nations.
in writing. for the last vote of this term, we are called upon to decide on the asylum package. this is the culmination of a process which has been going on throughout this parliament. while some progress has been made, differences between states still persist in the area of refugee recognition. i want to see the limitations that can be noted in the directive on the reception conditions for asylum seekers. it is again the member states who are in the forefront, to the detriment of the necessary european unity in this field. i hope that in the next mandate, at second reading, we will be able to reverse this situation and create a genuine european right of asylum that will provide genuine protection for these particularly vulnerable men and women.
in writing. all the reports on asylum voted today have a lax and extensive interpretation of the right to asylum, which will ultimately harm those who really need international protection to save their lives, their physical integrity or their freedom. the new social, financial, family and other rights that you want to impose on states to grant asylum seekers will become a vacuum pump for all economic immigration applicants, help to overwhelm the services in charge of these issues, further slow down the processing of files. because you repeatedly refuse to take account of the abuses and misuse of procedures, and you persist in confusing the rights and status that recognized refugees might have with the status you want to grant to mere applicants. but the most unacceptable is the lambert report, which creates a so-called european support agency, which will be able to distribute asylum seekers among the countries of the european union as it sees fit. we are not opposed to intergovernmental cooperation in these areas, with due regard for the sovereign right of states to decide who may enter their territory and under what conditions. but we are to your policies.

in writing. under the guise of fighting mafias and criminal organizations of all kinds, the brussels eurocrats still want to impose their federalist views that destroy nations, peoples and identities. while there is no doubt that each member state of the union has its own laws, legal traditions or codes, here is yet another attack by these fanatical euro-federalists: the desire to create a "european judicial culture". the european court of justice is the only institution in the world which has the power to decide on the legality of acts of the european union. what about the national law schools? what about the inextricable differences between the laws of customary law and those of written law? no answer is given, of course. in concrete terms, it is the entire judicial and criminal systems of the states which, in the face of this forced (i.e. bottom-up) harmonisation, will disappear. these sorcerer apprentices of europe have understood nothing, only the nation states, the basic elements of europe, can enrich it and give it back its full place in the world. europe must not be built at the expense of its nations and peoples.
in writing. we voted against this report firstly because it is without purpose: the treaty of lisbon does not exist, it was rejected in three referendums. secondly, because it advocates the subordination of national parliaments to the european parliament: the latter, because of its superiority and probably its unbearable arrogance, would support the national parliaments, which in its eyes are probably composed of ignorant and uneducated people, in examining european texts. support or pressure? would it invite itself to the plenary sessions of national assemblies, play the role of adviser, influence the way in which they transpose texts to encourage uniformity, impose itself to debate defence budgets... also dictate to them how they should monitor governments and their activities within the council? finally, because it is based on a double hypocrisy: the national parliaments have only been given a right of control which is very complicated to implement and therefore has little effect on compliance with the principle of subsidiarity; this principle is misleading, since many of the european union's so-called exclusive competences are sanctioned and the definition of subsidiarity given by the treaties de facto favours the powers of brussels.
in writing. the kaufmann report aims to provide guidance on how to implement a 'citizens' initiative', as defined in article 11 of the stillborn treaty on european union: 'at least one million citizens of the union, who are nationals of a significant number of member states, may take the initiative to invite the european commission, within the framework of its powers, to submit an appropriate proposal on matters for which they consider that a legal act of the union is necessary for the purpose of applying the treaties'. the report therefore sets out precise conditions for admissibility and concrete procedures which, incidentally, make it very difficult to bring such an 'initiative' to fruition. i want to warn the citizens here. this new "right" is a decoy. it provides only one thing: the possibility of asking the commission for new european laws, but not to repeal or change existing ones; not to change policies. and in any case, the commission has absolutely no obligation to listen to them. if the eurocrats are so keen to give rights to the citizens of europe, let them first respect their vote and finally understand that 'no' means 'no' in french, dutch, english, gaelic and all languages.

in writing. i voted in favour of the european parliament resolution approving the appointment of mr algirdas šemeta as a member of the european commission. i have, however, some doubts about the legal aspects of this decision. under article 215 (3) of the treaty establishing the european community, which lays down the rules in the event of a commissioner resigning, the council, acting by a qualified majority, appoints the replacement commissioner. the european parliament has, in my view, no power in this particular case, and its rules of procedure, which in annex xvii, point 2, second paragraph, provide for a secret ballot, are not in accordance with the treaty. this last article of the rules of procedure is binding on the european parliament but not on the commissioner who is duly appointed. article 214 (2) of the ec treaty, which is curiously mentioned as the legal basis for the resolution, does not concern the appointment of a commissioner in the event of his resignation, but the vote of approval of the commission as a whole as a college. it is also curious that this resolution was taken on the basis of rule 106 (4), which concerns the election of the whole commission and not the replacement of a commissioner.

council, and that is indeed the way we have gone forward. my colleague mr arif will not mind, i think, if i say that to suggest that i would sacrifice any industry, i find alarming or perhaps a little depressing, because that is certainly not the approach that i would take. do i think that if you want a serious trade deal you have to recognise that actually it is a deal where both sides benefit? yes, i do. if you want to have trade agreements, if we do believe – which i think we do – that trade is the engine that will take us out of recession, then it means you have serious, tough negotiations with industries and with countries that we care about having a deal with. otherwise we can just do deals all day long with countries we do not much care about, and we can open markets because we are not really interested. korea is a serious market. it provides real opportunities for chemicals, pharmaceuticals, other industries. we need to recognise the value and importance of doing this if we want serious trade agreements. we are, in fact, an economic superpower. i could not disagree more with my colleagues from the united kingdom when they talk about switzerland and try and equate that, somehow, with the relationship that we are trying to form in europe with korea – or maybe i just missed the point. this is about serious negotiations to get a serious outcome, and, as the details of this unfold, i hope that colleagues will look at it in the spirit that we have tried to set it up. the car industry gave us at the beginning a list of things that they wished us to achieve. they were genuinely very concerned to keep the market in korea open, and we have achieved all that they asked at the beginning. the textile industry: i am confident that there is little to worry about. the textile industry safeguards that we have will indeed make sure that we retain european jobs. i am not interested in closing down jobs or industries in europe at all, and this deal does not do that. and those of you who think that you have evidence to prove it, i ask you to supply it to me, because the rhetoric is one thing, the reality is a different thing, and we really have got to get beyond the rhetoric and into the reality of what this deal provides. indeed, i would argue that what we have got before us is very important for all the industrial sectors. the question about duty drawback is for me a very simple one. duty drawback is designed so that our response to it will prevent a particular problem. the question is, is it the only way of solving a problem? if there are other ways that equally solve the problem but in fact invite us to get a better trade agreement, then i will explore them. but i still want to solve the same problem, and i believe the mechanisms we have in place in this agreement do precisely that. it is not some thing that we hold up as being for ever enshrined as the only way of achieving what we want to achieve – to prevent, effectively, imports via the backdoor – and i believe we have resolved the problem in a different way. so i am not going to make apologies – politically, economically or in any other way – to parliament for having gone out and invested in negotiating this important trade deal. i make no apology for that, and i make no apology for putting forward to this parliament what i believe is a serious, 21st-century free trade agreement of enormous benefit across the economy of the european union. i especially make no apology for doing it at a time of economic crisis, because, if ever there was a time when my responsibility was to provide as much support for the businesses and the workers of europe, i believe that time is now, and that is what this deal does. i do urge colleagues, as i said earlier on, to look at the reality of the deal. you will be lobbied – i have been lobbied – but actually, when you look at what we have achieved, i believe it is a very concrete result that will hugely benefit the economy of europe. that, in the end, is what we set out to do, and that, in the end, is what we have achieved.
in writing. the european union-south korea free trade agreement (fta), which is due to be concluded by mid-october, is causing many concerns among european industries. the european commissioner for external trade considers this agreement to be the most ambitious ever negotiated by the eu, but car manufacturers in particular see it as highly unbalanced. the latter, because of the tariff preferences granted by the european commission, fear a massive influx of korean vehicles onto the european market. it is undeniable that the maintenance of certain customs clauses such as the duty drawback would be of an unenforceable nature and create a distortion of competition which would be highly detrimental to the european automobile industry. the eu's growth does not seem to have been offset by a reduction in the non-tariff barriers imposed by the korean authorities (import quotas on european petrol-engined vehicles). the commission must therefore, as of today, revise the terms of this agreement in order to restore the conditions for fair and fair competition and to ensure the maintenance of our industry and our jobs in europe.

acting president of the council. - mr president! - what is it? it is a great pleasure for me to be here today representing the swedish presidency. the presidency and the commission will jointly represent the eu at the g20 summit in pittsburgh on 24 and 25 september. we will hold an informal european council in brussels tomorrow to prepare the eu's common position. as you all know, the global financial crisis has necessitated unprecedented global action: first, rapid and strong fiscal and monetary policy measures to support the financial sector and the real economy. secondly, coordination of global action and the development of the g20's role as a forum for coordination, particularly of measures relating to the regulation of financial markets. the fiscal and monetary measures that could be taken quickly were absolutely necessary to get us through the worst of the crisis. the overall support to the eu economy this year and next is estimated at 5% of gdp. central banks have responded to the crisis by keeping interest rates near zero. today we are cautiously optimistic that the worst of the acute financial sector problems is behind us, but the economic situation is still unstable and the risk of a relapse is high. we are very much aware that rising unemployment will be a very dominant issue going forward. the situation is still uncertain, but it could have been much worse. international coordination and cooperation will be crucial to securing a broad recovery and setting the tone for a return to long-term, sustainable growth on a stable basis. the g20 has played and will play a central role in this. the g20 will also work with the international financial institutions, the imf and the world bank, to ensure that they have sufficient resources and a well-functioning internal organisation to support economic growth and safeguard financial stability worldwide. the g20 process has produced the following important results: firstly, we have a common analysis of the problems facing our economies. this may not sound like much progress, but a common view of the financial sector and the real economic problems behind the crisis is a prerequisite for effective countermeasures. secondly, we have made real progress with a series of concrete measures which we agreed in london at the summit this spring. this is the case, for example, with a comprehensive stimulus package for our economies and with increased cooperation on the supervision and regulation of financial markets. we have also ensured that the international monetary fund has sufficient resources to meet a demand for loans. we have also committed ourselves to improving the ability of international financial institutions to monitor the global macroeconomic situation in order to be able to give early warning of similar problems. much remains to be done, but we have made clear progress, driven through coordinated international commitments. i believe that we in the eu, together with the rest of the g20, have made great progress on a number of key issues which are crucial to be able to provide a strategic response to the economic and financial crisis. our coordinated eu strategy means that europe leads rather than follows the debate. it is our solutions that are taken into account when global solutions are being developed. that is why the presidency is inviting the heads of state and government to dinner tomorrow evening. the aim is to build on the successful work of the informal ecofin lunch and the g20 finance ministers meeting in london so that we come well prepared to pittsburgh. i expect that tomorrow's meeting and the summit in pittsburgh will continue to lead to progress on the overall issues i have mentioned, but also in some additional areas. one issue on which several european finance ministers have commented in strong terms is the role of bonus schemes in financial stability. there is a consensus among eu finance ministers that we should be leading the way in demanding effective global standards to ensure that bonus schemes do not have destabilising effects and that bonus payments are in reasonable proportion to performance. this is an important part of the overall effort to ensure greater transparency and better supervision in the financial sector and is crucial to ensuring future stability. the financial stability board has been asked to report to the pittsburgh meeting on its work on developing principles for bonus schemes. i hope that this report will contain concrete and practicable strategies to ensure that financial institutions put in place sound and responsible remuneration and bonus structures. in addition, i hope we can agree to continue to provide the necessary stimulus to our economies for as long as it is needed, but it is also important that we commit to discontinuing the measures when they are no longer needed so that we can return to balanced public finances when the recovery comes. we've just begun to reflect on these exit strategies. the design and coordination and the way they are implemented will be a very important component in achieving a balanced and long-term economic recovery. another major challenge is employment. we must carefully design the measures required, while ensuring a balanced interaction between fiscal and structural policies. i am convinced that we too will reiterate the need to stand up against protectionism and to ensure a level playing field in global markets. this will require significant coordination of financial regulation and supervision, but also of the winding-up of the extraordinary measures we have taken to support the financial sector. extensive work at national and eu level will still be required. discussions will continue tomorrow and in pittsburgh, but also throughout the rest of the year on the reform of the institutional financial institutions. we want them to be strong, with adequate resources, the right mandate, policy guidelines and governance structures that accurately reflect their membership. these issues are complex and interrelated, but they need to be addressed urgently so that financial institutions can carry out an increasingly important task. finally, i would say that there is of course a strong need for political determination to make progress in the discussions ahead of the copenhagen climate summit. this is a very important priority for the swedish presidency. we want to ensure that everyone has the right incentives to take action to limit global warming and to adapt economic policies to favour climate-friendly development. our goal is for the pittsburgh meeting to lead to progress on the guidelines for financing global climate action. i cannot promise that we will achieve everything we want because these are very complicated issues, but we promise that the presidency will responsibly present and defend the eu's positions. it is in this spirit that i look forward to fruitful discussions with the heads of state and government tomorrow evening and the concrete results that the world expects from pittsburgh next week. member of the commission. - mr president, mrs malmström, ladies and gentlemen, i address this house for the first time in this new legislature and i want to start by congratulating you all on your election, or re-election in many cases, and i am sure that i share with all of you the sense of responsibility with which we must face one of the greatest political challenges of our generation, which is to overcome this deep economic and financial crisis, to return to our citizens a horizon of confidence and stability, to widen the range of their opportunities and to achieve the highest possible level of social cohesion for all. the issue we are going to be debating at the g20 pittsburgh summit next week is at the heart of this challenge and this concern, and i am convinced that it will be a recurring theme throughout the next period, throughout this entire legislature, here in the european parliament, regardless of whether these issues are discussed at the g20 summits, in the european councils, in their own debates or in the own-initiative proposals that the next commission will bring to this house. the g20 summit in pittsburgh is the third summit of heads of state or government since the collapse of lehman brothers a year and a day ago and the beginning of a crisis of proportions unknown for many decades. in the light of the experience of the first two g20 summits at the highest level, in washington last november and in london this april, it is obvious that the g20 is playing a decisive role in coordinating the global response to this crisis. the g20's contribution to finding coordinated responses has been essential to preventing an even deeper recession than the one we are experiencing, and to laying the foundations for an economic and financial system that will prevent the future recurrence of the imbalances and excesses that have led to the present situation. the european union has played a key active role in activating the g20 to this end. the first washington summit was, as president barroso said yesterday, a european initiative of the french presidency, president sarkozy and the commission, and the european union also played a decisive role in setting the ambitious objectives of the previous two summits and in taking an active part in the preparatory work for them, in order to achieve not only declarations of principle but also concrete results and commitments. all of us europeans, the european institutions, should be satisfied with this. we can also be reasonably satisfied with the degree of coordination that has existed between the different european representatives in the g-20, the european countries that are members of the g-20 and participate in the g-20 meetings as such countries, plus the presidency of the european union together with the commission, which we represent the voice of all europeans and the common position of all member countries. the washington summit last november was the occasion for the world's major economies - the g20 countries representing something like 90% of the world's total gdp - to agree on the implementation of stimulus plans to sustain economic activity at a time, last autumn, when credit, international trade and investment were being brought to a standstill as a result of the very serious financial shock that first unleashed in august 2007 and accelerated in an incredible way in september 2008. a few days after the washington summit last year, the commission proposed the european economic recovery plan, which received the political support of the european council in december, and which has been the basis of the european response from the point of view of fiscal policies and policies to stimulate demand through instruments in the hands of national governments and parliaments, or in the hands of the european institutions themselves. with the latest information available, these discretionary fiscal stimulus, plus the play of automatic stabilizers, which in european countries is very important given the weight of our taxation and our social protection system, can be estimated to be adding, as a contribution to aggregate demand, the equivalent of 5.5 percent of the gdp of the european union between 2009 and 2010. the new us administration has also adopted a very important stimulus plan. since their automatic stabilizers are smaller than the european ones, the aggregate of the direct stimulus plus the automatic stabilizers leads to a similar boost on this side of the atlantic and the other side of the atlantic, but also countries like japan, china, canada and other g-20 members adopted equivalent fiscal stimulus. the london summit at the beginning of april this year stressed the need to implement these plans quickly, called for their careful monitoring and stated that, if necessary, they should be supplemented by additional measures. today we can say that the stimulus plans, together with the very substantial monetary stimulus also adopted by the central banks, plus the mobilisation of public resources in support of the financial institutions and, in particular, the banks, have succeeded in halting the free fall of the economy and allow us to see now, this autumn, the first signs of stabilization, as can be seen in the economic forecasts which i had the opportunity to present two days ago in brussels. for the first time in two years, these forecasts have not had to be revised downwards. however, we are not in a position today to ensure that economic activity can be sustained on its own if we withdraw the incentives. and it is true that there are, even with the stimulus that is being applied, risks of relapse given the extremely worrying progression of unemployment and the still unresolved weaknesses in the financial system. one of the messages that the g20 finance ministers, meeting in london earlier this month, have agreed to send to the pittsburgh summit is therefore the need to maintain temporary support measures for the time being, without prejudice to the need to devise a coordinated exit strategy now. and i will refer to that for a moment at the end of my speech. the two g20 summits in washington and london were also instrumental in setting a global agenda for reforms of financial regulation and supervision systems. we can say that we are witnessing a radical turning point after almost three decades dominated by the paradigm of deregulation and theories about the supposed infallibility of financial markets. in washington, the g20 countries laid the groundwork, set out the principles and defined the agenda for subjecting financial markets to stricter, more effective regulation and supervision, which does not leave areas, products or financial actors outside the scope of control of the supervisory and regulatory authorities, authorities that must cooperate and coordinate much more closely to overcome the flagrant ineffectiveness of national supervisory systems in the face of globalised markets and financial institutions that operate across borders in those markets. the london summit in april was a busy one, with concrete and significant progress being made in implementing this reform agenda. from prudential and accounting rules for financial institutions to the strong demand for transparency in non-cooperative jurisdictions, i.e. tax havens, to the regulation of hedge funds or other financial institutions, the organisation of transparent derivatives markets, or the enactment of rules on the remuneration of financial institution managers and traders operating in the markets, the london g20 gave a strong impetus to the fulfilment of the promise of reform. the european union has therefore not only carried out a very important task of promoting these agreements at the level of the g-20, but also an important task of implementing these g-20 agreements, which has meant intensive regulatory work for the last year. some of these proposals have already been adopted here in this parliament and by the council, others are now being discussed in this house and in the council and by the end of the year the commission is planning to adopt a further set of proposals, starting next week, the day before the pittsburgh summit, with the proposal to set up the european systemic risk board and the three european micro-supervisory authorities at european level, following the recommendations of the de larosière report which both the council and the commission have endorsed. the us administration has also unveiled an ambitious financial reform plan that president obama, this week, reaffirmed as a priority of his mandate, recognizing the responsibility of the united states as the place where this crisis was incubated and started. the pittsburgh summit set itself the objective of verifying that these reforms were making significant progress and of ensuring the necessary regulatory convergence on both sides of the atlantic. any regulatory divergence will or may in the future serve as a basis for investor arbitrage strategies that could again produce significant distortions in markets. but pittsburgh, in addition to monitoring the implementation of what has already been agreed and pushing forward the implementation of the measures adopted, must send a clear political message. it is now a matter of confirming the unwavering will of the states, political leaders, institutions, our countries, the european union, to establish a solid regulatory framework with a firm commitment and a dissuasive message: 'let no one think that once we have overcome the worst of this crisis, the previous practices that generated the crisis can be repeated, as if nothing had happened'. citizens want guarantees that financial institutions and their managers will be required to respect rules, particularly as regards remuneration, which prevent the financial system and the real economy as a whole from being put at risk again. and it must be said that the european union is totally united on this point. another issue which is high on the agenda of the various g20 summits is the reform of the international financial institutions to which minister malmström has already referred. i would just like to add that london has taken a step forward of enormous significance in terms of the financial capacity of these institutions and, in particular, of the international monetary fund, by increasing the fund's credit capacity by no more and no less than 500 billion dollars, bringing the total limit now available to the imf for its operations to 750 billion dollars. and in addition to this, it was agreed to distribute among all the member countries of the fund, in proportion to their quota, special drawing rights worth 250 billion dollars, and in addition to all this, it was also agreed to increase the financial capacity of the monetary fund to increase its concessional credits to the poorest countries. and all of this is already underway. in the space of six months much more progress has been made in this direction than in many previous years. the european union has, of course, agreed to contribute to this increase in the fund's financial resources, and the members of the european union have agreed to add eur 125 billion to their usual contributions to match the funding of the new objectives. the g20 leaders will also discuss the adaptation of the representation of the different countries in the governing bodies of the international financial institutions. the emerging and developing countries rightly aspire to more adequate representation. an aspiration which the european union supports, but which must be translated into concrete agreements, for which the european commission - which is not the official position of the presidency of the european union - continues to say that, in line with what this parliament has been thinking so far, the best representation of the european union in these bodies is a single representation. the pittsburgh summit agenda will also cover other issues: financing climate change, preparing for the copenhagen summit; the need to resume international trade negotiations and not give in to protectionist temptations; and strengthening support for the most vulnerable and weakest countries to deal with this crisis. as you know, the commission adopted a communication on climate finance last week. finally, let me conclude, noting the will expressed at the last meeting of the g20 finance ministers and which will be discussed at the pittsburgh summit, the need to lay the foundations for a future model of more balanced and sustainable growth. this is firstly achieved by devising exit strategies now, not to be applied immediately, but to be implemented when appropriate in a coordinated manner, because the determination of such strategies is not only key to a sustainable exit from this crisis, but also to offer at the same time a medium- and long-term sustainability horizon after the deep fracture that the crisis has taken on public finances, on employment levels and on the growth capacity of our economies.

mr president, commissioner, i welcome your determination to do so. europe has begun to put in place effective regulation, but it cannot be isolated. close international cooperation is necessary, and that is what we expect from the g20. it must continue with rigour and vigour the reforms which were initiated at previous meetings. the international regulatory framework for the financial sector needs to be improved so that it is in the service of investment, growth and employment. guiding principles must be affirmed. the crisis is not over. we must not go back to the situation we had before and abandon the measures needed to avoid, as far as possible, the recurrence of crises which are particularly damaging to the real economy, growth and employment. strengthening of supervision and regulation is also necessary. the supervisory obligations should reflect the level of systemic risk that financial institutions impose on the sector. speculative activities, which represent a significant risk, must be discouraged by increasing capital requirements and by applying the basel rules internationally. with regard to remuneration in the financial sector, it is appropriate to promote remuneration committees, to increase the transparency of remuneration through stricter publication obligations and to regulate variable remuneration, in particular bonuses. the strengthening of global financial institutions is also an imperative, as is the reform of governance and representation at the imf. these are, commissioner, some of the expectations of the citizens in the face of the next g20, where europe will have to speak with one voice, with strength and conviction.

acting president of the council. - mr president! - what is it? in the overall fight against terrorism, the question is how such activities are centrally financed. preventing the financing of terrorism and tracing the traces that transactions may leave can both prevent and be important in the investigation of terrorist offences. to do that, we need to work together internationally. we should follow the call of the 1999 un convention on the prevention and punishment of the financing of terrorism and the relevant council of europe conventions. members who attended the hearing behind closed doors on 3 september 2009 in the libe committee heard how the terrorist finance tracking programme (tftp) has contributed to increasing security also for eu citizens. in recent years, information from the tftp has contributed to the detection and investigation of terrorist offences and also to the prevention of terrorist attacks on european soil. the presidency has a unanimous negotiating mandate from the council of 27 july 2009 based on a proposal from the commission. the best thing would have been if the negotiations with the united states had been based on the lisbon treaty. the european parliament could then participate fully, but as you know, that is not possible yet. since swift is moving its database from the us to europe at the end of the year, it is imperative that the eu conclude a short-term agreement with the us as soon as possible so as not to risk an interruption in the exchange of information. it's in everyone's best interest. i would like to emphasize that this is an interim agreement for the interim period until a permanent agreement can be concluded. it will not last longer than 12 months and as soon as a new treaty is in place the commission has announced its intention to submit a proposal for a permanent agreement. in order to benefit the eu and the member states, the us must continue to provide the respective competent authorities in the eu with information from the tftp in the same way as it has done so far. it will happen. in addition, the interim agreement will explicitly allow eu law enforcement authorities to request data from tftp databases themselves in the context of terrorist investigations. the presidency is convinced of the usefulness of the tftp data. at the same time, we are clear that the interim agreement must contain the necessary mechanisms to guarantee the protection of the individual's privacy, legal certainty and data protection. the draft agreement therefore contains a provision that a specific eu authority will receive, process and approve a request from the united states to obtain information from swift. equally important, the interim agreement will contain detailed provisions on data protection in respect of the information received by the united states from swift through the european authority. the agreement will go further than in the past through the unilateral commitments to the eu entered into by the us in the so-called tftp representations of 2007, published in the official journal of the european union. let me mention a few additional provisions which we will be demanding that the agreement contain. data shall be stored securely, any access to data shall be logged, any search of the tftp database shall be limited to persons or data where there is a well-founded suspicion or a clear link to a terrorist offence, the retention period of the data reviewed shall be limited and data shall be deleted from the database at the latest after five years and earlier where possible. we are very clear that the tftp should only be used in investigations of terrorist offences, including the financing of terrorism. the system can be used by the us or the eu to investigate other types of crime or for other purposes. it is also important, of course, that the transfer of information from the eu to the us under the tftp is proportionate in the agreement. that is why, in addition to the rules on the european authority which i have just mentioned, there is a provision that the system is to be evaluated by an independent evaluation group. this group consists, for the eu, of representatives of the presidency, the commission and two persons from the national data protection authorities of the member states. the evaluation team shall be responsible for reviewing compliance with the agreement, the correct application of the data protection provisions and the proportionality of the transfer of data. we have a shared responsibility to ensure that law enforcement agencies can work effectively against terrorism. we also have a shared responsibility to ensure that this is done in a legally secure manner and with respect for fundamental rights. the presidency is convinced that the exchange of information with the us under the tftp will increase protection against terrorism and that we can reach both an interim and eventually a long-term agreement that meets our high standards of data protection and respect for fundamental rights.
vice-president of the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would first like to thank mrs beatrice ask warmly for giving us an update on all the developments concerning swift and on the negotiations currently under way with the united states for the continuation of the programme to track down terrorist financing, the tftp. i myself had the opportunity, at the libe committee meeting on 22 july, to explain how the tftp works and why we need an interim solution to ensure that it does not come to an end. the joint meeting of the libe and econ committees on 3 september was attended by the swedish presidency, jls director-general mr faull and mr bruguière. i believe that this meeting has helped to clarify a number of open questions. i would like to emphasize a few aspects briefly. the added value of the us treasury's evaluation of data under the tftp was confirmed by mr bruguière's report, which was read by the members of the libe and econ committees at the joint meeting in early september. as the presidency also recalled, this data analysis has enabled the us authorities to prevent attacks or to facilitate investigations into terrorist attacks, both in the us and in europe. on the other hand, the report by justice bruguière confirmed that the us authorities had respected the commitments made in 2007 in the field of data protection, namely - as béatrice ask has just pointed out - the limitation of data retention and access to be used only if there is a suspicion of terrorist financing. in short, mr bruguière said that the commitments had been respected. however, it is clear that the legal framework negotiated in 2007 will no longer be operational as soon as the data is no longer in the us, following the change in swift's architecture planned for the end of the year. in order to allow the us authorities to continue to analyse data on these inter-european transactions located in the netherlands, an interim international agreement between the eu and the us is necessary. the inclusion in this agreement of all the guarantees necessary to safeguard the fundamental rights of our citizens, in particular the protection of personal data, is an absolute prerequisite. of course, we fully support the presidency in its efforts in this direction. i would also like to say to parliament, mr president, as the minister has just said, that this is an interim agreement, which cannot exceed a maximum of 12 months, and which must be renegotiated immediately after the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon, with the full involvement of the european parliament. i can assure you that the commission will of course continue to keep parliament constantly informed of developments in this matter. i would add that we are happy to be able to prepare this agreement, which will be a permanent agreement, a lasting agreement, requiring, of course, perfect reciprocity from our american partners. we are also interested in the fight against terrorism and there is no reason why there should not be full and complete reciprocity. that is why i believe that parliament's participation in the negotiation of a future lasting agreement will be beneficial. that's what i believe, in my soul and in my conscience. i would like to thank the swedish presidency and mrs beatrice ask again for having explained to us the situation which is now involved in this agreement, which is again temporary.

in writing. the principle of non bis in idem - the same person cannot be tried twice for the same facts - is a fundamental principle of law in a democracy. i myself am a victim in france of its violation, still being prosecuted on the orders of the government in a case where i was nevertheless totally acquitted by the court of cassation. i owe this in particular to the failure of mrs wallis, the rapporteur on my immunity, who accepted all the devices to remove me from the protection to which i was entitled, if the rules of justice, morality and the case law of this parliament were followed. but mrs weber's report is not intended to avoid such double prosecutions. there is a european convention for this purpose dating from 2000 which seems to be working to the satisfaction of practitioners and in compliance with the rule of law. no, the weber report is essentially aimed at giving eurojust, which many would like to see transformed into a european prosecutor's office, powers of control and decision-making over national courts. that is why we voted against it.

madam president, like many of my colleagues, i fully support mr coelho's report and i thank him very much for the excellent work he has done. from the outset, the reason for the abolition of internal border controls, the sine qua non of the abolition of internal border controls, was the existence of compensatory measures to avoid the much feared security deficit. they are the basis of the mutual trust which is essential for the proper functioning of schengen cooperation. it is therefore only with an effective and transparent evaluation mechanism of the application of the schengen acquis that we can maintain this trust and therefore a very high level of cooperation between the states. the stakes are therefore high and parliament's role in creating this new mechanism must be commensurate with the stakes. it will therefore have to be adopted by codecision, at least as regards the first pillar, if this text is to be adopted before the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon. moreover, while it is certainly necessary to draw the consequences of the integration of the schengen acquis into community and union law, the commission should not be entrusted with the management of this evaluation alone. states must be more closely involved in this evaluation mechanism. otherwise, the mutual trust could be eroded. it is the internal security of our states that is at stake. when one state fails to apply this acquis correctly, all the other states suffer the consequences. finally, in terms of efficiency, it does not seem to me appropriate to provide for two separate mechanisms for each of the two evaluation phases, namely the pre-application control and the application of the acquis by the schengen states. i therefore join carlos coelho in asking the commission to withdraw this proposal and to present a new one which takes greater account of the philosophy of the acquis and the role of the states in assessing its application.
vice-president of the commission. - madam president, i also want to thank mr simon busuttil very much for his excellent report. the six third countries - antigua and barbuda, the bahamas, barbados, mauritius, saint christopher and nevis and the seychelles - were transferred from the negative to the positive list of regulation (ec) no 539/2001 by a new regulation 1932/2006 adopted on 21 december 2006, which confirmed that those countries fulfilled the criteria laid down in that regulation. that regulation made the implementation of the exemption from the visa requirement for nationals of those countries conditional upon the conclusion and entry into force of a bilateral visa exemption agreement between the european community and each of those countries. as simon busuttil said, full reciprocity had to be ensured, because some of these countries still required visas for citizens of one or more member states at that time. due to the temporary visa regime applied by caricom the caribbean common market countries to nationals of several member states during the cricket world cup, formal visa waiver negotiations were not opened until july 2008. in order to ensure that citizens benefit from the visa exemption as soon as possible, the commission proposed the provisional application of the agreements which were signed on 28 may 2009 and since that date they have been applied provisionally pending the completion of the procedures necessary for their formal conclusion. on the basis of the principle of reciprocity, the exemption from the visa requirement applies to all categories of ordinary, diplomatic or official service passport holders, irrespective of the purpose of the journey, with the exception of the pursuit of a paid activity. in order to ensure equal treatment for all citizens of the union, as mr busutill has said, the agreements contain a provision which provides that the six third countries may only suspend or terminate the agreement in respect of the citizens of all the member states of the european community, and reciprocally that the community may only suspend or terminate the agreement in respect of all its member states. i thank parliament, i thank mr busuttil for his cooperation, which is support for this initiative which will facilitate the mobility of our citizens, and i add that in this somewhat cold parliament we can dream of visiting sooner or later all these wonderful countries, such as the seychelles or the bahamas...

madam president, climate change, as we have been saying since this morning, is simply the worsening of desertification and drought, deforestation, natural disasters, the increase in hunger and poverty, mainly in the southern countries, and migration flows. the copenhagen summit must benefit from the commitment of the nations of the world to strike a balance between four important objectives, the first of which is, of course, to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, but also to not slow down our economy, to avoid ecological dumping and to promote new european technologies. so, in this connection, as we must take the poorest countries into account, i would like to draw your attention to the developing countries, particularly the most advanced developing countries. this concept does not appear in international texts and these countries are included in the category of developing countries. they are therefore not considered as countries that should contribute to the effort to reduce greenhouse gases, even though they are among the largest consumers of carbon. i am thinking, of course, of china, i am thinking of india, i am thinking of brazil, which absolutely must commit themselves in copenhagen to similar goals to those of the industrialized countries, because they have absolutely nothing in common with most of the other developing countries. the co2 reduction efforts must be allocated under the most equitable conditions. we must avoid any distortion of competition. the negotiations must also be an opportunity to stimulate the deployment of our new technologies, to enable significant funding for research and development. in copenhagen, it will be necessary - and it is a necessity - to create the conditions for a sustainable exchange between countries, based on mutual interests. the success will be to promote the dissemination of technologies to the least developed countries in return for the recognition of intellectual property rights and the opening of markets for these technologies.

the rapporteur. - mr president, i would first like to take this opportunity to thank president barroso and commissioner šemeta for having decided to postpone the publication of the commission's proposals on future budgetary policy and on the update of the financial perspective until the next half-year. the european council and the parliament had agreed that this update should take place in 2008-2009, but that was four years ago, which is an eternity. in the meantime, there have been the treaty of lisbon, the first irish referendum, the financial crisis, the delay in the entry into force of the new treaty, etc. it is therefore wiser to entrust the new commission with the task of presenting its political programme and the financial version of it at the same time, in a few months' time. however, since the lisbon treaty will come into force on 1 december next, we need to adopt very quickly the transitional measures necessary to move from one treaty to another in the budgetary field. the swedish presidency has proposed that the conciliation committee on 18 november should be the occasion for a political agreement between the three institutions on this subject. it is therefore up to parliament today to give its delegation to the conciliation committee a negotiating mandate. four points must be settled in a very short time; the commission has already made a number of proposals. first, the transfer procedure: the abolition of the distinction between compulsory and non-compulsory expenditure requires the adoption of a single procedure, placing the two budgetary authorities on an equal footing, without compromising the necessary flexibility of management by the european commission. secondly, the additional budgets: from the beginning of 2010 an initial additional budget will be needed to give all the institutions concerned the financial means to exercise the new powers provided for by the lisbon treaty. we therefore need a simplified procedure, inspired by the new procedure provided for in the treaty for the main budget itself. thirdly, the timetable for preparatory meetings between the three institutions, which we call the pragmatic timetable: this is an area where we do not need to innovate in relation to previous practice. fourthly, the procedure for using the provisional twelfths formula in the unlikely but still possible event that we do not reach agreement on the 2010 budget: on this point, it seems to us that the provisions of the lisbon treaty are sufficiently precise that no supplement is necessary. your committee on budgets adopted these proposals by a very large majority. i would ask the house to do the same, so that we can conclude the negotiations with the council and the commission in due time.

in writing. prior judicial authorisation: this is what we wanted to obtain. with this compromise we have at least guaranteed the best possible legal protection at this stage. the eu's message is now clear: internet access is a fundamental right, and precise and binding procedures will have to be followed for an internet user to be effectively prosecuted for copyright infringement. it is now up to national judges and the judges of the european court of justice to ensure that the right of every internet user to a 'fair and impartial preliminary procedure' is respected. the lack of clarity of many provisions will require close monitoring in the transposition process and in the application of this important legislation. the european parliament, as a co-legislator, will now be able to continue to defend net neutrality, as the lisbon treaty has now been ratified. today's vote is just one step in a long process. we will have to continue to defend the "rights of internet users" and in particular better define them. we will also have to deal urgently with the crucial issue of copyright on the internet.
in writing. i abstained on this final version of the telecoms package because it is not satisfactory. it is better than nothing, though. it does not protect internet users from the abuse of liberticidal laws, such as the hadopi law, first version, in france, nor from the wrath of administrative authorities duly mandated to do so. it does, however, give them legal means to defend themselves. it is a disgrace that we have to come to this: relying on the european union, which makes a mockery of the opinion of the citizens, and whose vast majority of acts are essentially in the interests of lobbies of all kinds, to guarantee a minimum of freedom of information and expression to europeans.
in writing. as the telecoms sector is experiencing unprecedented growth, it was essential to support my colleague catherine trautmann's report, which will provide consumers with better services at fairer prices. i welcome the fact that this text will strengthen the rights of users to universal services, through clearer contracts, a more accessible emergency number, a hotline for missing children, better consideration of the rights of disabled people, and the assurance of the portability of the number. it will also help to better protect privacy and combat illegal practices on the internet by improving the security and integrity of electronic communications networks. finally, it is welcome that a legally sound solution has been reached which offers european citizens procedural safeguards such as the right to be heard, the presumption of innocence and the right to be heard, and which requires states to respect them before any measure to restrict access to the internet.
in writing. it is clear that the proposed compromise between the council and parliament does not offer sufficient legal protection for users. while the text states that end-users of the internet cannot be restricted by member states, it opens the way for consumers to be restricted by access providers without a prior decision by a court. this reality is a violation of human rights. the amendments tabled by our group to defend the rights of citizens were not accepted. finally, the package is subject to the internal market 'law'. the european court of justice will therefore decide on 'conflicts of interest'. freedom of expression would thus be subject to the law of the internal market, as all too recent examples show. thanks to strong pressure from users and citizens, protections for users have been won, however they remain insufficient for the left. we cannot accept compromises on the rights of citizens to express themselves.

acting president of the council. - mr president! - what is it? i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. i want to begin by thanking you for the opportunity to come here today to discuss this important issue. judging by the questions raised by some of the members, it is clear that this is a matter of some concern. i hope that today i can clarify the council's position on this matter and answer your questions. the rule of law and respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms are fundamental principles of cooperation within the european union. they shall guide the cooperation of the member states within the union. these principles are and will continue to be the basis for cooperation in the area of asylum and migration. eu cooperation on migration has developed rapidly in recent years and covers a wide range of legal acts and other types of action. as regards the rights of asylum seekers, i would like to point out the fundamental purpose of asylum cooperation. the aim is to create a common european asylum system, which provides protection for people in accordance with the geneva convention relating to the status of refugees and other international treaties relating to people in need of protection. within the framework of cooperation, there are provisions for the provision of subsidiary protection, provisions on the asylum procedure, reception and return. the provisions cover the whole of the asylum field and form the basis of the common european asylum system. the most important legal acts in the field of asylum are the dublin regulation on criteria and mechanisms for determining the member state responsible for examining an application for international protection, the reception directive, which sets minimum standards for the reception of asylum seekers, the protection grounds directive, which concerns minimum standards for determining when a third-country national is considered to be in need of international protection, and the asylum procedures directive, which sets minimum standards for the procedure for member states to grant or withdraw international protection. all these acts are currently being reviewed with a view to further approximating the legislation of the member states in this area and thus making it more complete and effective. the proposed amendments will be decided by the co-decision procedure, which will give us a broad political anchor for the development of the common european asylum system. well-managed migration involves both creating opportunities for people to enter the union legally and for returning those who do not fulfil the conditions for entry and stay on the territory or who lack grounds for asylum. as regards the fundamental rights of those who do not have the right to reside in the union, i would like to refer to the general principles of law which should be the basis of all eu action and, more specifically, to the rules governing the return of third-country nationals who do not have the right to enter or reside legally in a member state. the return policy is based on the principle of mutual recognition of the right to return. the directive is an important first step towards legislation aimed at providing fair and transparent procedures to achieve a more effective return policy at european level. the return policy should be based on the principle of legal certainty, humanity and effectiveness. the return work also includes provisions on joint return flights. the council decision on the organisation of joint flights for the return of third-country nationals who have not been granted a residence permit or asylum was adopted in 2002 under the return action programme. the organisation of joint flights is resource-efficient and contributes to improving operational cooperation between member states. i would like to stress, however, that this is not the enforcement of collective expulsion decisions, but a cooperative measure to make more effective use of the capacities of the member states. the common guidelines accompanying the council decision provide that joint flights may be organised for persons who do not or no longer fulfil the conditions for entry, stay or residence on the territory of a member state. the organising member state and the participating member states shall ensure that the legal situation of each of the returnees for whom they are responsible allows for the return. the regulation establishing a european agency for the management of operational cooperation at the external borders of the member states of the european union also allows this authority, namely frontex, to provide the member states with the necessary support to organise joint return operations. in october this year, the european council also called on frontex to examine the possibility of financing joint return flights. all these measures are designed to ensure that international protection is available to those who need it and that the return of illegally staying third-country nationals is carried out in a legally secure and lawful manner. the use of joint return flights does not constitute a breach of the principle of non-reform or a circumvention of the requirement of an individual examination. member states are expected to take into account the specific circumstances of each person subject to return, including any application for international protection. this of course also applies to people who have come from afghanistan. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. the community's return policy is of course important, but it is only one aspect of an overall migration policy. the european pact on immigration and asylum, adopted by the european council last september, reaffirms the union's commitment to the global approach to migration. this means that migration issues should be an integral part of the eu's external relations and that effective management of migration must be consistent. it also requires a close partnership between the countries of origin, transit and destination. the stockholm programme, which we discussed earlier this afternoon, will of course confirm and further develop this overall strategy.
the commission's vice-president - mr president, i will try to recall the main principles governing our attitude to these problems of migration and return. eu law requires member states to ensure that third-country nationals present on their territory can apply for international protection if they so wish. as regards the possibility of these nationals, in this case afghans, being granted some form of international protection, member states must examine each asylum application by applying the criteria laid down by european legislation to the particular circumstances of each applicant. member states must determine whether the asylum seeker qualifies for refugee status and, if he does not meet the criteria required to be considered a refugee, whether he is eligible for subsidiary protection. i'll call you back principle by principle. first, third country nationals should not be returned to their country if they are exposed to serious harm. eu legislation, and in particular the so-called 'qualification' directive on asylum, states that member states must respect the principle of non-refoulement in accordance with their international obligations. so member states cannot return to afghanistan people who are refugees in the sense of the geneva convention or who have been granted subsidiary protection. in addition, member states are required to ensure that no return operation is carried out in breach of article 3 of the european convention on human rights, which obliges member states to ensure that a person is not returned to his or her country if he or she is likely to suffer persecution or serious harm on return. secondly, we cannot generalize the demands as to whether it is appropriate to conduct rescue operations to afghanistan. afghanistan is one of the main countries of origin for asylum seekers in the european union. it should be added that the union is, however, hosting only a small fraction of the total number of refugees from afghanistan, most of whom are in neighbouring countries, notably iran and pakistan. general conclusions cannot be drawn as to whether the forced return of afghans to their country of origin would violate community law, the european convention on human rights or the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. it is for the member states in which applications are submitted to decide on each application in the light of its particular characteristics. when examining applications, member states should examine the relevant individual circumstances in order to determine the possible protection needs of each applicant. this requires an examination of the political, security and human rights conditions prevailing in afghanistan. this also requires consideration of the particular situation in the part of the country from which the person concerned originates, as well as the particular circumstances of that person, such as his or her family environment, activities in the country of origin or any other specific characteristic which may make him or her more vulnerable. there are no general conclusions on the protection needs of afghan asylum seekers, but statistics show that the recognition rate for them has increased in recent months. in the first half of 2009, almost 50% of afghan asylum seekers received international protection in the european union, compared to less than 30% in the last quarter of 2008. i now come to another question. what are the conditions to be met before deciding to carry out a re-conduction operation? in my recent statement on the joint uk-france operation to return afghans to kabul, i said that before returning an individual to a third country such as afghanistan, member states should take three precautions. they should, first, have ensured that the migrant concerned does not wish to apply for international protection; secondly, if an application for international protection has been lodged, ensure that the application has been thoroughly and individually examined and rejected after an appropriate evaluation procedure; thirdly, to ensure that the life of the migrant returned to his country of origin is not endangered. the commission sought further clarification on the circumstances of this french and uk operation to resettle afghans. however, the commission has no evidence at present that these three conditions have not been met by the persons concerned. what about those return operations involving several returnees, provided that the case file of each of them has been assessed individually? protocol iv to the european convention on human rights and the charter of fundamental rights of the european union prohibit collective expulsions, but there is no legal obstacle, nor indeed any objection in principle, to several individual return measures being carried out jointly, each on the basis of a separate decision, for example by using the same flight. there is also no legal obstacle to such operations being organised jointly by several member states. the current mandate of frontex already provides for operational cooperation in the field of joint resettlement operations. the european council has asked that the operational capabilities of frontex be strengthened and that in particular consideration be given to the possibility of regularly chartering aircraft to carry out these operations. these joint operations should improve the efficiency of the rescue operations from a logistical point of view and perhaps also benefit from a number of very desirable accompaniments, since rescues are always painful. the commission has also noted that, while the return directive has not yet been transposed by most member states, the commission nevertheless encourages member states to ensure now that their decisions on readmission comply with the standards set out in the return directive. this includes giving priority to voluntary returns, providing for remedies against return decisions and taking into account the specific needs of vulnerable persons. this return directive is not yet applicable. it will be soon and it will still provide some additional guarantees for those concerned. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. of course, billström also explained that in all these problems we try to keep a fair balance between the willingness to welcome those who are persecuted for political reasons and who really deserve protection, and then at the same time the need to also recognize that some requests have no reason to be accepted. there is therefore a difficult balance to be struck, which the commission is careful to maintain. i can say that to parliament, listening of course to the speeches which will follow this presentation.
on behalf of the ppe group. mr president, the union must give a dignified welcome to people fleeing war and persecution and offer them international protection schemes in line with its values. however, the european union has for several years been faced with mixed migration flows and smuggling networks that abuse national asylum systems to bring in people who do not meet the conditions required to avail themselves of them. so what do you do? this question has arisen in each of our member states. the capacity of the state to absorb is not unlimited. protection schemes must be offered to people who meet objective criteria, and if we want to maintain our tradition of being host countries, it is essential to be firm against the diversion of these asylum procedures for the purpose of economic migration. it is also important to note that all countries targeted by illegal immigration channels from afghanistan or iraq implement forced return measures. they're forced to. it is enough to mention a number of member states of the european union which are putting them into practice, regardless of their political colour. there is no longer any political disagreement within the union on these issues and it is this consensus which will make it possible, in the very near future, to implement joint removal operations financed by frontex. this initiative, as a common tool for managing migration flows, should be welcomed. i would also like to point out that collective expulsion operations are entirely distinct from collective expulsions within the meaning of the case law of the european court of human rights. the strasbourg court forbids any measure compelling foreigners as groups to leave a country, but it authorizes cases where such a measure is taken after a reasonable and objective examination of the particular situation of each of the foreigners. international and european refugee law is sufficiently dense to ensure that these deportation procedures are strictly regulated and that they are carried out in compliance with the fundamental principle of the dignity of the human person.

i would like to thank mr vital moreira for his speech. on 9 december, the euro-mediterranean trade ministers will meet to discuss the relaunch of our economic and trade cooperation. first of all, i would like us to make a clear statement together. while the objective of the free trade area was to benefit all partners, north and south, setting its coming into being in 2010 was neither realistic nor even desirable, given the still-existing development differences between the northern and southern shores of the mediterranean. in addition, some have repeatedly argued that in order to advance the euro-mediterranean process - which, i would remind you, is composed of the three pillars: political, economic, social and cultural - it was necessary, in the face of political difficulties, simply to set them aside in order to make progress on the economic and commercial side. this magical and pernicious vision that trade alone can make progress towards harmonious integration, peace and stability, as you have understood, i do not believe in. i don't believe in it, especially since the facts speak for themselves. the union for the mediterranean, for example, by putting aside political conflicts, was supposed to revive stagnant euro-mediterranean cooperation by means of so-called concrete and visible projects. today, the union for the mediterranean is stagnating, and the political disputes that have been overlooked are a stark reminder of it. i am one of those who remain fiercely attached to the spirit of barcelona, of those who believe that progress is not measured solely by trade statistics, which are still too unfavourable to our partners in the south, to their populations. trade for trade, no, i definitely do not believe in that. on the other hand, trade in the service of development with the aim of reducing wealth disparities, genuinely shared prosperity or regional integration, yes, i understand that. but the negotiations must be guided in this direction. that is why, at this next meeting, i call on us to be collectively ambitious, not to be content with mere technical discussions with the removal of barriers to trade as the objective. it is no longer acceptable that this logic persists. regional integration, particularly in its south-south dimension, the responses to the economic crisis which is hitting hard with its corollary of job losses, considerations of human, social and environmental development and the question of human rights must feed the discussions and return to the heart of our concerns.

the doha negotiations were opened in 2001 to redress the imbalances, indeed the injustices, of the international trading system established at the end of the uruguay round when the wto was set up. it was thus recognised that the uruguay round had not fulfilled all its promises to developing countries and that the trade rules were not fair to the countries of the south, particularly in the agricultural field, because they allowed the richer countries to both protect their markets and continue to subsidise their production, including for export, thus ruining many farmers in the south. cotton has become the symbol of this situation. in opening the "development cycle", wto members have therefore committed themselves to correcting multilateral trade rules to ensure that trade actually benefits the economic and social development of all countries, on all continents. it should therefore always be borne in mind that this round of negotiations is not a round like any other and that, even if, as in any negotiation, everyone expects progress on the subjects of interest to him - for the industrialized countries, industrial products and services - it was understood from the outset that this was first of all a round of rebalancing in favour of the developing countries. today, after the seventh ministerial conference, as before it, the negotiations are stuck, essentially on the slopes of capitol hill in washington, as they were yesterday in the sands of cancún, and, at the time, this was largely due to the demands of the european union. by imposing their own demands during the negotiations, the industrialized countries have thus jeopardized the conclusion of the negotiating round and the very credibility of the wto. each one is focusing on its own particular objectives instead of focusing on the overall objective of creating a multilateral trading framework based on fairer rules to enable fairer trade, and which contribute to sustainable development and poverty eradication. the first result of this deadlock is the proliferation of bilateral trade agreements, which are often even more unfavourable to the countries of the south. it's a regression, you know? the european union must therefore take a clear stance. the priority is to conclude this cycle as a cycle of development and not to outbid on industrial products and services. we must not approach this negotiation with a traditional, narrow-minded approach, where each party is simply seeking its own advantage. this leads to a deadlock and misses the point: the need to create a new regulation of the international trading system, which is part of the new global governance that everyone has called for, especially after the g20, to meet the real challenges of today: equitable development of all continents, the eradication of poverty, food security, respect for social rights and decent work and the fight against climate change. the european union must show how, in these negotiations, it is ensuring that the rules of trade contribute to this in the future. this is the angle in which each of the points of discussion should be viewed: on agriculture, respecting the commitments of july 2008; conclude the negotiations on the modalities; guarantee, in particular, special and differential treatment, respect for special products, safeguard mechanisms; to develop agricultural aids towards sustainable agriculture and food security; on products covered by the amna, request tariff reductions from the developing countries i conclude which are compatible with their level of development; the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the future of the eu's external relations.
