acting president of the council. - mr president! - what is it? what we call restrictive measures is something very important and i know that many members have their views on it. that may be a little difficult for those listening to this debate to understand. let me begin by describing how the council uses these measures. then i will come to the treaty of lisbon. restrictive measures against third countries, individuals, natural or legal persons or other entities are an important tool of the eu's foreign and security policy. in general terms, they are used to bring about a change in a particular policy or activity. they should, of course, be used as part of an integrated, comprehensive policy which may include political dialogue, various forms of incentives and conditions to be met. restrictive measures alone are not always sufficient to bring about change, but they can be a means of putting pressure on repressive regimes, stopping the flow of money and other resources that support such regimes or terrorist networks. in some cases, restrictive measures are imposed by the council when we implement resolutions adopted by the un security council under chapter vii of the un charter. in such cases, the various eu legal instruments must strictly adhere to these resolutions. it concerns situations and acts, including terrorism, that pose a threat to peace and security. they can only be part of the eu's external action and are therefore different from the action to create an area of freedom, security and justice, which is our objective within the union. the council interprets the treaty of lisbon as meaning that we apply article 215 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union to these and other restrictive measures in the framework of the common foreign and security policy, including in relation to terrorism. the eu can also decide to apply additional measures in addition to those decided by the un, and we can also introduce measures on our own. sanctions decided by the eu on its own initiative may be imposed to support other foreign and security policy objectives respect for human rights, democracy, the rule of law and good governance all in accordance with the eu's obligations under international law. today, measures are usually directed directly against those identified as responsible for the policy or measures being targeted, or against their interests or sources of income. this is more effective than broad sanctions in the form of general trade embargoes or other more arbitrary measures. targeted sanctions are designed to minimise the negative consequences that may result for the population of the country concerned. this aspect is very important when the council is preparing a decision to impose new sanctions. all penalties are reviewed regularly to evaluate their effectiveness. they can be adjusted or cancelled altogether, depending on the development. under the lisbon treaty, restrictive measures are also a continuing tool of the common foreign and security policy, through council decisions under article 29 of the treaty. an important change introduced by the new treaty is that decisions on restrictive measures affecting natural and legal persons are now subject to judicial review. this means that the court can review the legality of a sanction decision. it wasn't like that before. with the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon, regulations are adopted on the basis of a joint proposal from the high representative for foreign affairs and the commission, in accordance with article 215 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union. the european parliament shall be informed of such a decision. i understand that this change is not welcomed by parliament, since the council is no longer obliged to consult parliament on sanctions affecting individuals. but that is how we interpret the treaty. it is important to point out that any decision on restrictive measures, and their implementation, must always be in accordance with international law. restrictive measures imply restrictions on certain rights of the individuals against whom they are directed. the sanctions must therefore, of course, respect human rights and fundamental freedoms. this concerns procedural rights and the right to legal protection. the measures must also always be proportionate to the objective. with the experience we have gained in applying sanctions, we have made careful assessments and looked at how to apply sanctions in a good way. a number of concrete improvements have been introduced. this includes the criteria for the application of certain sanctions, but also the reasons for the listing of an individual, a natural or legal person or other entity. this must be reviewed continuously and adapted if necessary. in this work, the council has taken account of the european parliament's resolution of last year on the evaluation of eu sanctions as part of the eu's human rights policy.
vice-president designate of the commission. − mr president, as the presidency said, the questions you have put forward raise important issues in relation to the future management of restrictive measures or sanctions in the eu. following the entry into force of the lisbon treaty we now have to make a choice as regards the legal base for the proposed regulation which amends the al-qa’ida and taliban sanctions regulation. our view is as follows: firstly, the new treaty has added a specific provision to the article in the former ec treaty on foreign policy-related restrictive measures or sanctions. article 215(2) provides a new legal base for restrictive measures against natural or legal persons and groups or non-state entities. it expands the scope of the former article 301 and should be applied as the legal base for amendment of the al-qa’ida and taliban sanctions regulation. secondly, article 215 applies when there is a common foreign and security policy (cfsp) decision. the al-qa’ida and taliban sanctions regulation implements a cfsp decision which requires that regulations be made to implement certain un security council resolutions. these resolutions are binding for eu member states under international law. thirdly, we consider that a double legal base – article 215(2) and article 75 – is not workable. that is because the objectives, scope and procedures of the two articles are different. i note that parliament’s legal affairs committee and legal advisers have made the same assessment. in conclusion, it is our view that the new treaty has provided specificity and clarity on the legal base for restrictive measures against natural or legal persons and groups or non-state entities. article 215 addresses the role of parliament and council and the legislator should not deviate from the treaty. we were also asked to provide information on fundamental rights-related improvements in the work of un sanctions committees. the proposed amendment of the al-qa’ida and taliban sanctions regulation implements the findings of the european court of justice in the kadi case. in that judgment the court made a number of comments on ways to improve the listing procedures applied by the un al-qa’ida and taliban sanctions committee. the points made by the court are the motivation to amend the listing procedures of the regulation. a number of un security council resolutions have set out the procedures for handling the sanctions list at un level. most recently, un security council resolution 1822 provided that a summary of reasons should be made available on the un al-qa’ida and taliban sanctions committee’s website in connection with each listed person, and provided for a review of all names on the list by 30 june 2010, with provision for regular review thereafter. the resolution demanded that the relevant state take measures to inform the listed person of their listing, the reasons for it and information about exemptions and delisting requests. the approach in resolution 1822 has since been replicated in resolution 1844 on sanctions in relation to somalia and in resolution 1857 in relation to democratic republic of congo. resolution 1822 provides for a review of the measures contained in it after 18 months. that period expires at the end of this year. work is ongoing in connection with the review but the commission is not in a position to indicate what changes to the procedures the un security council will decide.
for the greens/efa group mr president, i am talking here about targeted sanctions, as they are called, smart sanctions, those which also have a direct impact on the fundamental rights of individuals, organisations or legal entities of any kind. and these basic rights are important. this can be, for example, freedom of movement, but also protection of property. and for these reasons, these targeted sanctions must meet a number of minimum procedural standards and legal certainty. i would add that compliance with these legal and procedural standards is essential to the very credibility and therefore to the effectiveness of these targeted sanctions. it was the parliamentary assembly of the council of europe - we remember this in this house - which, through the voice of one of its parliamentarians at the time, dick marty, called for transparency and the right of defence, and showed the absurdities of this lack of transparency in the effectiveness of the listing and delisting, which could also affect innocent people who themselves were not aware of their situation and were unable to respond to the situation they discovered, generally by chance. that is why access to data, as mentioned by louis michel, the communication of the elements that justify the listing, protection in the transfer of personal data, are essential elements of this procedure. secondly, it took great perseverance on the part of the victims of the un and eu sanctions system and the mobilisation of civil society, human rights organisations and also the european parliament to have their rights recognised by the court of justice of the european communities. and the amendments proposed by the council on the black lists depend on the proposals that have been made, including by the european parliament. that is why the european parliament must be absolutely involved in these decisions, in their implementation and in their control, since history shows that it was the european parliament which made possible the reform of the council regulation.

mr president, the greens/efa group believes that cohesion policy is at the heart of one of the most structural approaches of the european union: solidarity. europe is strengthened whenever european solidarity is expressed. this is a fundamental question for us. we believe that the european commission must incorporate the following principles: firstly, since territorial cohesion is a political priority, it must also be a budgetary priority. secondly, the region is the relevant level of partnership for a regional development policy. we cannot accept the renationalisation of this policy. thirdly, cohesion must also be used to bridge the most serious economic and social gaps within a single territory, to the benefit of deprived urban areas or, in the direction of rural areas in difficulty or very poorly served due to structural handicaps, such as islands. finally, all the regions of the union must be eligible for cohesion policy in a differentiated way, of course, according to their level of wealth, but the european union must be able to make its contribution whenever cohesion policies are at stake.
